item.title: Arista Warns of Critical VeloCloud SQL Injection Zero-Day Exploited in Attacks (2026)
item.description:
Attackers are exploiting a zero-day SQL injection flaw in Arista's VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), the central management system for VeloCloud SD-WAN networks, the company said in an advisory on October 22.

The flaw lets anyone who can log in to the orchestrator, even with a read-only customer account, gain operator privileges, the top level of control over it.

For on-premises orchestrators, the fix is in VCO 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10, and 6.4.2.12, while Hosted and Dedicated orchestrators have already been patched.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-114625 and rated 9.9 on the CVSS scale. Orchestrators running the releases that fixed the VCO flaws exploited in July and September are still affected, because those releases are older than the new fixes.

Arista bought the VeloCloud SD-WAN product line from Broadcom, announcing the deal in July 2025. The products were earlier known as VMware SD-WAN by VeloCloud.

To exploit the flaw, an attacker needs network access to the orchestrator's web interface and a valid login. The minimum role is Enterprise Read Only, the lowest built-in role for customer users. VCO is exposed by default, and no VCO setting prevents the exposure.

In VCO, operators create the customer and partner accounts, and each partner can manage a group of customers. The flaw allows an attacker to act as a local superuser, a role with full access. It may also allow an attacker to affect the VCO host itself and expose, modify, or disrupt the orchestrator and the data it manages.

The advisory does not say when the attacks began, which orchestrators were hit, or what the attackers did after exploiting the flaw.

The new flaw is the third in VCO since late July that Arista has reported as exploited, and the first of the three that requires a login. Neither the July flaw (CVE-2026-16812) nor the September flaw (CVE-2026-93952) needed one.

Affected and Fixed Releases

Each affected release train has its own fix, shown here beside the release that fixed September's flaw on the same train.

Release train Affected by CVE-2026-114625 Fixed in CVE-2026-93952 (September) fixed in
5.2 Before 5.2.3.18 5.2.3.18 and later 5.2.3.16
6.1 Before 6.1.3.10 6.1.3.10 and later No fix listed
6.4 Before 6.4.2.12 6.4.2.12 and later 6.4.2.8

VeloCloud Gateway and VeloCloud Edge are not affected. The 7.0 release train is not on the list, and Arista says any release not on the list is not vulnerable.

Arista has not checked releases that have reached end of support. Customers on an unsupported release train can contact Arista's Technical Assistance Center (TAC) about upgrade options.

As of October 22, September's flaw is fixed only in the 5.2 and 6.4 trains. On 6.1, it affects releases up to 6.1.3.7, and no fixed release is listed. Neither advisory says whether 6.1.3.10 also fixes the September flaw.

If You Cannot Upgrade Yet

Until the fixed release is installed, Arista recommends these steps:

  • Limit access to the VCO web interface to trusted administrative networks.
  • Monitor the VCO for connections from known malicious IP addresses.
  • Watch for unexpected outbound network activity from the VCO host.
  • Consider blocking outbound ports that normal operation does not need.
  • Watch for backdoor daemons and webshells.
  • Review recent administrator activity for unexpected changes.

Checking for Compromise

Two IP addresses have been seen carrying out the attacks, according to Arista. Block them and check logs for any sign of them:

  • IP: 74.82.197[.]86
  • IP: 38.54.50[.]151

Also check VCO web access logs for requests with unusual URL-like path components, encoded characters, references to local or internal services, or high request rates.

If you suspect a compromise, save evidence before fixing anything, where possible. That means the VCO web access, backend application, system and database logs, along with the relevant file-system timestamps.

Regarding the July and September flaws, Arista warned that a compromised orchestrator could also grant attackers access to VeloCloud Edge devices. For this flaw, the advisory does not say whether the risk applies or whether upgrading removes access that an attacker has already gained.

item.title: The AI Agent Nobody Owns: Watch Expert Webinar On Your Newest Insider Threat (2026)
item.description:
Right now, there is probably an AI agent running on a laptop somewhere in your network. It stores API keys and database passwords, can access your internal systems, and works without anyone watching.

Nobody reviewed its access. Nobody owns it.

If an employee had that much reach with that little oversight, you would call it an insider risk. So why do we still call the agent a productivity tool?

Most of the conversation about AI security is about what threat actors are doing with it. But the bigger threat may already be inside your organization.

That's the focus of our upcoming webinar, AI as an Insider Threat: From Shadow AI to Governed AI, with expert guest Richard De La Torre, Technical Product Marketing Manager at Bitdefender. Save your seat for a practical security playbook on bringing that unseen AI under control.

Where AI is hiding on your endpoints

It isn't only developers. AI agents, coding assistants, MCP servers, and browser extensions are turning up across the business.

And most of them never cross your network gateway in a way the tools you already run would recognize.

The result is a hard irony. The AI with the most access is often the AI your security team can't see.

📅 Save Your Spot: Watch the Webinar

The visibility gap, by the numbers

According to Bitdefender's 2026 Cybersecurity Assessment report, only 51.8% of organizations report having full visibility into the AI tools their staff use. That leaves nearly half without the full picture.

That blind spot has a cost. IBM found that 20% of breached organizations were compromised through shadow AI.

Which raises the question: what can organizations realistically do about it? That's exactly what the webinar gets practical about. Register now to see what a lean team can do about the AI it can't yet see.

From shadow AI to governed AI

New research from Bitdefender Labs looks at what's really running on endpoints, based on real machines; among the findings: a malicious agent skill caught in the wild.

Blocking AI outright is the obvious response, but it tends to fail. The alternative is governed adoption, and the session shows what that looks like in practice.

What you'll take away

  • Where AI is actually showing up on your endpoints, and why the tools you already run don't see most of it.
  • New research from Bitdefender Labs on real machines, including the malicious agent skill caught in the wild.
  • Why an AI agent with credentials and no owner behaves like an insider risk, and what to do about it.
  • Why blocking AI outright tends to fail, and what governed adoption looks like instead.

The AI already running on your endpoints won't wait for a policy. Join expert guest Richard De La Torre, Technical Product Marketing Manager at Bitdefender, and save your seat for AI as an Insider Threat.

item.title: PHP2Shell Exploit Attempts Hit Millions as Attackers Try to Deploy Mirai Malware (2026)
item.description:
Threat actors have been observed unsuccessfully attempting to exploit the newly disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to rope infected systems into a Mirai botnet variant called Potassium, as it emerges that weaponizing the flaws may be harder than previously thought.

The attacks aim to exploit CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2), which can result in unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) via specially crafted HTTP requests. The vulnerabilities have been patched in PHP versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

"However, analysis of the sample revealed that it is an updated and significantly expanded version of the Mirai-derived botnet variant identified in early 2026," Sophos said. "The sample displays downloader and network disruption functionality."

⚡ WARNING — PHP Warns of Another Unpatched RCE Flaw CVE-2026-115560

Specifically, it resolves a hard-coded, encrypted command-and-control (C2) address, establishes a TCP connection to 134.199.154[.]64, and sends an HTTP request. The malware then checks for an HTTP 200 response status and verifies that the resulting payload begins with the ELF magic bytes 7F 45 4C 46, indicating that it expects a Linux ELF binary as a follow-on payload.

"A resolver function supports IPv4 addresses and hostname resolution, with additional fallback resolution logic that includes hard-coded public DNS servers such as 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, and 1.0.0.1," Sophos added. "As with Mirai malware historically, this sample can execute DDoS attacks."

The attacks have been found to originate from the following three IP addresses -

  • 85.11.167[.]243
  • 217.60.242[.]76
  • 45.198.224[.]169

These attack sources have been found to contact 92.118.112[.]100 to retrieve a loader, which is responsible for deploying the Mirai botnet variant. Further analysis of the artifact within a network-contained sandbox has revealed that the botnet issues a DNS query for thunder.godofthunder[.]st, resolves it to 134.199.154[.]64, and establishes a C2 channel on TCP port 50792.

The end goal is to launch sustained volumetric flood attacks against two adjacent hosts located within a single Ukrainian network -

  • 45.88.138[.]0
  • 45.88.138[.]44

The lack of a successful attack leveraging PHP2Shell in the wild suggests that threat actors are "struggling" to come up with reliable exploits, Sophos added.

Potassium was first flagged by botnet tracking platform Synthient in March 2026. In a follow-up analysis, Nokia Deepfield researchers described the malware as a Mirai fork which uses "ChaCha20 for the static config table (the first time we have seen ChaCha20 used this way in a Mirai variant), a single static byte (0xED) for everything on the wire, a named reverse-shell protocol (SHELL / SHOUT) on the same channel as attack commands, and a DNS misdirection scheme that swaps the two 16-bit halves of every resolved A record before connect()."

Arctic Wolf, which also shared additional details of the same weaponized PHP2Shell exploitation attempt, said the botnet supports 24 commands to facilitate flood attacks over ICMP, TCP, UDP, and OpenVPN protocol. Both builds for ARM and x86 also contain configuration for resolving C2 infrastructure through Ethereum Name Service (ENS).

"ENS resolution was disabled in both samples, indicating that the capability was present but inactive," the cybersecurity firm said. "If enabled in future variants, it could complicate disruption by reducing reliance on registrars and DNS providers, requiring defenders to block the ENS names, RPC infrastructure, and resolved command-and-control addresses."

Threat Actor Mass Exploits PHP2Shell

The development comes as SOCRadar said it found PHP2Shell exploit tooling for PHP 8.4.26 on an exposed attacker-controlled server ("206.188.197[.]105:9999"), alongside three screening scripts that check live websites for preconditions the PHP2Shell chain depends on.

The scripts, according to the cybersecurity company, checked about 20 public websites for the PHP version, server setup, and session settings the exploit needs. These websites span Canada, China, Finland, France, Poland, the U.K., and the U.S.

"The central file, aslr_exploit.py, is a Python exploit the operator labels a 'one-click' PHP2Shell exploit for PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php," SOCRadar said. "It works entirely over ordinary HTTP requests in three broad steps: it recycles the target's PHP worker, leaks memory addresses through the session cookie to defeat address space layout randomization (), and then abuses PHP's session upload progress handling to run a shell command."

ASLR, short for Address Space Layout Randomization, is a cybersecurity mechanism that randomizes the memory locations used by system files and programs each time they are run, making it harder for attackers to predict where code will load. This built-in defense helps defend against memory-based exploits, such as buffer-overflow attacks.

The other three companion scripts are as follows -

  • php2shell_fp.py, which reads PHP version and server setup from about 20 sites
  • deep_probe.py, which examines 11 of those sites for visible errors, phpinfo pages, file inclusion, and session injection to ascertain whether they meet exploit prerequisites
  • wp_attack.py, which focuses on five WordPress sites to conduct user and plugin enumeration

That said, there is no evidence of shell access on any screened site as of October 22, 2026, indicating the targeted sites did not meet the exploit's preconditions.

The toolset is assessed to be part of a broader operation that involves the attacker extracting API keys and backend URLs from websites' client-side JavaScript, systematically sweeping web and API routes for unauthenticated access, and using a pool of rotating proxies to spread traffic and evade rate limits and blocking.

"Related artifacts on the server additionally point to web-archive reconnaissance and automated CAPTCHA solving," SOCRadar noted. "Taken together, the toolset points to a financially motivated actor focused on cryptocurrency and Web3 targets."

The same exploitation server ("206.188.197[.]105") has also been flagged by Hunt.io, which said the threat actor behind the operation has targeted 123 servers across cloud, shared-hosting and ISP networks. "About 57 run PHP, many on unsupported 5.x to 7.x," the threat intelligence firm said. "Ten rejected the request outright, including three of the five sitting behind Cloudflare. None was exploited."

In all, 10 open directories hold PHP2Shell-related tooling -

  • 206.188.197[.]105
  • 102.210.149[.]166
  • 122.10.110[.]72, 122.10.17[.]49
  • 58.221.60[.]160:8000
  • 41.223.30[.]7, 157.230.117[.]70
  • 104.219.251[.]31
  • 107.150.31[.]151
  • 217.160.132[.]82
  • 47.100.125[.]108, 54.169.109[.]7, 139.162.165[.]136

Defeating ASLR Protections

The disclosure also coincides with the development of a PHP2Shell exploit that can achieve remote code execution on ASLR-enabled x86-64 systems with PHP's recommended production configuration.

"One of the biggest obstacles has been address space layout randomization (ASLR), a protection designed to make memory corruption vulnerabilities much harder to exploit," Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, told The Hacker News.

"Our team developed a novel technique [...] that chains the two vulnerabilities together, using a memory leak to bypass ASLR and achieve remote code execution on x86-64 systems, even with PHP's recommended production error-display setting."ir

"We haven't identified another public or commercial exploit that achieves this under the same conditions. Developing this capability was far from trivial, but it demonstrates that a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on production-configured systems can be overcome."

Consequences of successful exploitation of the flaws are severe, as it permits an attacker to execute code with the permissions of the web application, potentially gaining access to API keys, database connections, and other internal services the application can reach, VulnCheck said.

"An attacker doesn't necessarily need administrator or root access to cause significant damage," McIntyre said. "Access to a vulnerable web application could provide a foothold into other parts of an organization's infrastructure."

Exploit Attempts Plenty, None Successful

The findings dovetail with reports indicating that broad exploitation attempts targeting the flaws are underway, including by a China-based IP address that has been observed trying to drop a web shell via a server-side session file.

Web infrastructure company Cloudflare said it observed tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw 45 minutes after the flaws were publicly announced, before climbing to hundreds of thousands within 2 hours and millions as of early October 22, 2026.

"So far, most of the activity is scanning, along with some uncoordinated attempts to deliver various payloads," Cisco Talos said. "This is expected: scanning or basic exploitation with public proof-of-concept (PoC) code takes far less effort than integrating a vulnerability into an actor's own tooling."

Data from Previdian's telemetry has so far recorded hundreds of exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-109618 from dozens of IP addresses, and against CVE-2026-109619 to a lesser degree. The first exploit event aimed at CVE-2026-109618 was recorded on October 21, 2026, at 1:05 p.m. UTC.

"We've seen plenty of PHP2Shell probes and exploitation attempts in our honeypots," Previdian said. "At the time of writing, we've observed no successful remote code execution and no dropped PHP files. Reliable RCE may be harder to achieve than initially expected."

This assessment has also been echoed by Beelzebub, Dataminr, and Wordfence, with observed activity so far limited to scanning, fingerprinting, and attempts to confirm command execution, steal credentials and secrets from environment variables, install persistent access, and retrieve and execute a second-stage payload.

Wordfence has shared the following IP addresses as among those attempting to exploit the flaws -

  • 87.121.84[.]174
  • 181.215.186[.]252
  • 185.196.220[.]132
  • 185.161.210[.]29
  • 152.233.51[.]69
  • 45.134.225[.]16
  • 107.189.14[.]87
  • 193.47.62[.]24
  • 2409:40d2:204e:4be:2a1f:f9c9:a055:e00b
  • 103.147.220[.]17

The severity of the flaws has also led to several government, school and hospital websites going offline across Asia, Europe, and North America out of an abundance of caution. The U.K. government has confirmed that 32 digital services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable, largely stemming from the precautionary shutdowns while security updates and mitigations were applied. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has issued approximately 50,000 warnings to businesses and other organizations.

"The vulnerable code dates back to PHP 5.4, released in 2012," the Sysdig Threat Research Team said. "The bugs live in the PHP engine, not within any application. For that reason, any WordPress, Drupal, or Joomla site with clean application code is still exposed."

With the fixes not available for older versions of PHP, PHP2Shell is expected to have a long tail, along the lines of Log4Shell. According to estimates from Google-owned VirusTotal, about 272,000 hosts run a supported PHP branch (8.2 to 8.5), Organizations on PHP 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1 are advised to move to a supported branch, or use a distribution backport.

Attack surface management platform Censys said it currently detects over 4.18 million hosts and 67.5 million web properties running PHP. Of these, more than 34.4 million PHP services are still assessed to be vulnerable as of October 23, 2026.

"Many applications with web servers and similar will likely remain vulnerable until their respective vendors patch these items," Dataminr said. "The implications of this are that many organizations will likely remain vulnerable to some degree for far longer than when patches are directly applied to owned and managed applications."

(The story was updated after publication to revise Censys's host and web property counts based on its improvements to PHP detection logic.)

item.title: Critical x402 SDK Flaw Could Let Malicious APIs Drain AI Agents’ Token Balances (2026)
item.description:
AI agents paying for API calls with the x402 SDKs could sign a payment for their full balance of a supported token if a malicious API asked for it, security firm V12 said on October 22.

The cause was the SDKs' default client, which set no spending limit until releases on August 18 added one. The risk was limited to agents who automatically signed payments and whose apps set no limits.

The missing limit is one of 25 flaws V12 found in the x402 code, and one of three it rated critical and described in detail. The x402 Foundation, which maintains the SDKs, had already fixed all three critical flaws in the August 18 releases.

One of the other two let a facilitator, the service that checks x402 payments, accept a Solana transaction that moved no tokens as a valid payment. Among the x402 SDKs, only the TypeScript one had this flaw. The other let a malicious server get an agent to sign a login message for a different website.

V12 found the flaws by reviewing the code and running local tests. Neither V12 nor the x402 Foundation has publicly reported any attacks using them.

The foundation has published no security advisory for the three flaws, and its changelogs list the fixes without calling them security fixes. As of October 23, npm audit returned no advisories for the last TypeScript releases before the fixes, and PyPI listed no vulnerabilities for the last Python release before them, The Hacker News found. A developer who relies on those checks gets no warning to upgrade.

Coinbase created x402 and handed it to the x402 Foundation this year, a Linux Foundation project whose members include Visa and Mastercard. Coinbase holds the most senior seat on the foundation's technical steering committee.

No Spending Limit in the Default Client

x402 is an open standard that lets software, including AI agents, pay for an API call within the web request itself, without requiring a person to approve each payment.

A server that wants payment answers with the HTTP status code 402 Payment Required and lists its payment options, each with an amount, a token, and a recipient. The client picks one, signs a payment, and sends the request again.

The default client took the first option on the list, and before the fix, it set no limit on the amount.

A hostile API could use that to turn a routine data request into a request for the wallet's full balance of a supported token, V12 said. An earlier small payment could reveal the wallet address, so the server could look up the balance first.

With an automatic signer and no payment policy set by the app, the client could sign a payment for that amount. For a token that supports signed transfers, the attacker could then submit the signed payment and collect the funds.

The August 18 releases added spend controls to the TypeScript, Python, and Go clients. By default, they now cap each payment at $1 and allow only US dollar stablecoins the SDK recognizes, such as USDC.

Token Approvals Accepted as Solana Payments

In x402, a merchant's server relies on a facilitator to check each payment and submit it to the blockchain. On Solana, the facilitator also pays the transaction fee.

The TypeScript facilitator code for Solana checked that a payment called an allowed token program, then read it as a transfer without checking the instruction type. A token approval, which lets another account spend tokens later but moves none itself, differs from a transfer only in its first byte.

In V12's local test, the facilitator accepted such an approval as a valid payment. The test did not send a live transaction.

A merchant relying on the facilitator could therefore deliver a paid resource while receiving no tokens, V12 said, calling it "a complete payment bypass." The attacker needed a token account, but no balance, and the facilitator paid the transaction fee each time.

The Python and Go SDKs already checked the instruction type. The August 18 releases added the same check to the TypeScript code.

Every published @x402/svm release from 2.0.0 to 2.22.0 lacks the check, and every release from 2.23.0 on has it, The Hacker News found by searching the published packages.

Logins Signed for Other Websites

x402 also has a sign-in extension called Sign-In-With-X (SIWx). It lets an agent log in by signing a short message with its wallet, for example to prove an earlier payment instead of paying again. On Ethereum, the message names the website, the wallet address, and a one-time code.

The automated client signed these messages without verifying that the website named in them was the one it had contacted.

A malicious server could get a fresh login message from another site, pass it to the agent, and use the signature to log in to that site as the agent's wallet, V12 said. That would work wherever the other site accepted the relayed message, and the attacker would get whatever access the login allowed.

The August 18 releases make the TypeScript, Python and Go clients refuse to sign unless the site in the message matches the site that sent the 402 response. The project also changed the SIWx specification, which now says a client must refuse to sign when the two do not match.

TypeScript code that calls createSIWxPayload directly must now pass the URL of the 402 response, after any redirects. The @x402/fetch and @x402/axios wrappers pass it on their own.

What to Update

Upgrading to the latest releases also brings later fixes, including one for a separate payment bypass in @x402/core 2.27.0 in September. As of October 23, the latest versions are 2.28.0 for @x402/core, @x402/svm, @x402/extensions, @x402/fetch and @x402/axios, v2.28.0 for the Go module and 2.25.0 for the Python package.

In TypeScript, clients get the spending fix by updating @x402/fetch or @x402/axios to 2.23.0 or later, which pulls in the matching @x402/core. Apps that use SIWx also need @x402/extensions 2.23.0 or later, which holds the login check. Facilitators that check Solana payments need @x402/svm 2.23.0 or later.

After the upgrade, existing clients are capped at $1 per payment and limited to recognized stablecoins unless the app sets its own spend controls. Apps that pass spendControls: false turn all of these controls off.

Teams that cannot upgrade yet can register a payment policy that drops any option above a set amount. The older clients support this with registerPolicy in TypeScript and Go and register_policy in Python, which also has a ready-made max_amount policy.

V12 advises clients to check that a SIWx login message identifies the site they contacted before signing, to set budgets for each payment and in total, and to limit which tokens, networks, and recipients they will pay.

item.title: Researchers Demonstrate Node2Shell RCE Exploit on Node.js Build Using Crafted Brotli Data (2026)
item.description:
Malicious Brotli data can make an application on an official build of Node.js run attacker-supplied code, security researchers at Imperva have demonstrated.

Their "Node2Shell" proof of concept ran code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image for Linux arm64, with no debugger or custom build, by feeding crafted data to the bundled Brotli decoder (CVE-2026-111497). Node.js disclosed the flaw and released fixes on October 21, and applications that decode untrusted Brotli data should update.

Imperva's test did not succeed on every attempt, and code execution took several tries in its Linux arm64 setup. The result covers that one build and application setup, with other architectures and the 22.x and 26.x lines not tested. On the fixed release, 24.22.1, the same data was rejected, and no code ran.

The demonstration goes beyond the first public proof of concept, which achieved code execution only on a deliberately weakened test build. On a standard build, that proof of concept's author reported a crash and a limited read of process memory, not code execution, and said a working attack on a normal build was not achieved.

No exploitation of the flaw in the wild has been reported as of October 22.

Which Applications Are Affected

The flaw is in the Brotli decoder that Node.js bundles, so it affects applications on the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines, not only the one build Imperva tested. A service reaches that decoder from either side of an HTTP exchange: when it reads a Brotli-compressed response through Node.js's built-in fetch(), or when middleware decodes a Brotli-compressed request body.

Express 5's body parsers, such as express.json(), express.urlencoded(), express.text() and express.raw(), now decode Brotli request bodies when applied to a route, alongside gzip and deflate. A plain Node.js HTTP server does not decode a Brotli request body just by receiving one, so the decoding needs that middleware or an explicit call.

Imperva reproduced code execution through both the request-body and response paths, testing Express 5.0.0 to 5.3.0 and body-parser 2.0.0 to 2.3.0 at pinned versions, and did not test every release in between.

How the Bug Works

Imperva traced the cause to how the decoder handles an impossible point in a Brotli stream: the stream announces the block types it will use as decoding runs, and the test input reached a block change that the stream's own structure ruled out. The vulnerable decoder read that as a request for more input and kept going in an invalid state.

In a separate test with a memory sanitizer, continuing from that state wrote past an intended buffer, the out-of-bounds write behind the flaw.

Node.js fixed the flaw by importing an upstream Brotli patch that makes the decoder stop with a format error at that point instead of continuing.

What to Do

The fix is to move to a patched release. The update should reach container images and other artifacts that bundle a Node binary, which a package inventory can miss. End-of-life lines 20.x and earlier do not receive the fix and should be moved to a supported line.

The advisory lists no workaround inside Node.js, so an application that cannot update at once has no fallback in the runtime. Imperva suggested limiting untrusted Brotli traffic on affected paths where that is practical, and said only the update removes the flaw. The company also added rules to its own web application firewall and tested them against the attacks it reproduced.

Vercel, which runs Node.js for its customers, said it added rules on October 21 that block the attack in inbound requests. The rules do not cover Brotli responses an application fetches from other servers, and do not replace updating.

item.title: Critical Flaw in Python’s Popular Pillow Image Library Allows Code Execution via a Crafted Image (2026)
item.description:
Pillow, the most widely used image library for Python, can be made to run operating system commands on a server by specifying the name of a file it is told to open.

The flaw, CVE-2026-112900, is in the way Pillow handles EPS images, which it opens by passing the file's name to Ghostscript, a separate program it runs to turn the image into pixels, without checking the name first.

Ghostscript can read a name chosen by an attacker as instructions rather than as a file, and point it to a second file that carries commands to run. Pillow's maintainers fixed it in version 13.0.0, released on October 16.

Pillow turns up almost everywhere Python handles images: web upload forms, avatar and thumbnail tools, document and PDF pipelines, and most machine-learning projects pull it in. OX Security, the firm whose report drew attention to the flaws, estimates the library is downloaded about 436 million times a month.

Version 13.0.0 is a large security release, with fixes across four severity levels, from low to critical, two of which are rated critical by the maintainers. None of the flaws is known to be under attack.

The weakness is the filename, not the picture. "The flaw is triggered by the filename, not by anything in the PostScript document," the advisory says, meaning a harmless EPS file can still cause damage when an attacker sets its name. That makes upload endpoints that keep or build a stored file's name from user input the realistic target.

The flaw only reaches Ghostscript on hosts that have the gs program installed, which Pillow needs to open EPS at all. It affects Pillow from version 2.6.0 up to 12.3.0.

The maintainers rate it moderate, because the attacker has to control the filename. The CVE record assigned by GitHub rates it 9.2 out of 10 and marks it as the same condition.

Two of the fixes sit in the maintainers' top "critical" tier. One is a separate memory bug, described in the release notes as stale image data reused after a mode change. The other covers two overflow flaws in Pillow's JPEG decoding.

One of those JPEG flaws, in the FlashPix (FPX) format, was shown to run an attacker's command from a single call to Image.open() on a crafted file, as long as the optional olefile package is installed. Pillow recognizes these files by their content, not their extension, so a server that opens untrusted uploads can be hit with no user action.

The other, CVE-2026-112403, overflows a memory buffer when a program makes a thumbnail of a crafted lossless JPEG. Its advisory reports a crash, not code execution. The bug was "found by Anthropic using Claude to study the security of open-source software, validated manually by Ada Logics," the advisory says, part of a wider effort by the company that has turned up hundreds of flaws in open-source libraries.

A third flaw, CVE-2026-112393, has been in Pillow since 2013. It overflows a memory buffer when a program saves a compressed TIFF image to memory rather than to a file on disk, the common pattern for a service that re-encodes an upload and hands it back. The advisory says the reporters crashed the process with it, and turned it into code execution only with the help of a second, separate flaw that leaked memory addresses. Saving to a real file on disk is not affected.

The CVE records, assigned by GitHub, score the EPS, TIFF, and JPEG-thumbnail flaws 9.2 out of 10, a critical rating. Each depends on conditions the score does not carry, and the maintainers' own ratings for the batch run from moderate to critical. In the CVE records, CISA's analysts mark no known exploitation for the EPS flaw and a public proof of concept for the TIFF one.

What to do

Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0, which fixes all of these, and rebuild any containers, wheels, or base images that bundle an older copy. Pillow 13 drops Python 3.10, so installs still on 3.10 need Python 3.11 or newer as well.

pip install -U "Pillow>=13.0.0"

Until you can upgrade, Pillow's security guidance and the advisories point to steps that cut each path:

  • EPS / Ghostscript: keep the gs program off any host that processes untrusted uploads, and never pass an attacker-controlled filename to Image.open() for EPS.
  • JPEG thumbnails: avoid draft() and thumbnail() on untrusted JPEGs, or call load() first, or pass reducing_gap=None.
  • TIFF: treat saving a TIFF to an in-memory buffer such as io.BytesIO as a sensitive path when the image came from a user.

item.title: Russia-Linked Hackers Used New Mesh Network Backdoor in Destructive Ukraine Attack (2026)
item.description:
The Russian state-sponsored hacking group Sandworm teamed up with another threat actor to carry out a destructive wiping attack targeting a Ukrainian logistics company last year.

According to ESET, the attack involved UAC-0099 (aka Earth Sirrush) obtaining initial access to the target on July 16, 2025, via a spear-phishing email bearing a malware-laced attachment that led to the deployment of the MATCHWOK backdoor through a downloader called MATCHBOIL.

The activity ultimately concluded with the threat actor handing off access to Sandworm, which then conducted a data-wiping attack on September 17, 2025, more than two months after it obtained a foothold.

What makes the attack stand out is UAC-0099's use of a previously undocumented backdoor called MythicRatatoskr that communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server hosted inside the Yggdrasil mesh network. The backdoor was deployed a day after MATCHWOK was executed.

There are indications that development on the backdoor started sometime between December 2024 and February 2025. Its functionality is fairly straightforward in that it sends victim metadata to the C2 server, polls for new commands, transmits command output, takes screenshots, and uploads/downloads files.

It can also alter the current working directory, enumerate directory contents, change the C2 server URL, execute a shell command via "cmd.exe," and spawn a reverse SOCKS5 proxy. In addition, some artifacts include a 10-minute startup delay in a likely effort to avoid immediately connecting to the Yggdrasil network and evade detection.

"To our knowledge, this is the first documented case of Yggdrasil being abused in this way by a state-aligned threat actor, and it may signal a broader trend of adversaries adopting experimental peer-to-peer networks to increase the resilience and stealth of their infrastructure," ESET researchers Anton Cherepanov and Peter Strýček said.

MythicRatatoskr is said to have been used to deploy a SOCKS5 server to route connections through the compromised network. The attack culminated with Sandworm carrying out a data-wiping attack by dropping the SDelete utility via Active Directory Group Policy. It's worth noting that the Sandworm-linked NikoWiper malware is also derived from SDelete.

Yggdrasil map with the C&C server

While the attack investigated by ESET compromised a Windows environment, source code references to "crond" within MythicRatatoskr suggest there possibly exists an equivalent Linux version of the malware.

The assessment that UAC-0099 is likely collaborating with Sandworm is not new. In its APT Activity Report Q2 2025–Q3 2025, ESET said it observed UAC-0099 conducting initial access operations and subsequently transferring "validated targets" to Sandworm for further post-exploitation.

These attacks targeted government, energy, logistics, and grain sectors in Ukraine, the Slovak cybersecurity company noted at the time. ESET confirmed to The Hacker News that the MythicRatatoskr case was among those attacks.

This sort of cooperation between Russia-aligned actors is also not new. Last year, ESET said it identified evidence that Gamaredon and Turla were working together to target and co-compromise Ukrainian entities, with one intrusion leveraging Gamaredon's PteroGraphin to deploy Turla's Kazuar backdoor.

Furthermore, a Gamaredon-linked downloader called Pterodo has been used to retrieve and execute InvisiMole, a modular spyware program put to use against targets in Ukraine and Russia.

"This kind of cooperation underscores the potential for coordinated cyber espionage campaigns among Russia-aligned groups, likely intended to amplify their operational impact," ESET said.

item.title: PHP Warns of Another Unpatched RCE Risk Two Days After Emergency PHP2Shell Patches (2026)
item.description:
PHP has warned of another way an attacker could run code on a web server, two days after it shipped emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell flaws.

The new issue, assigned CVE-2026-115560, affects only web applications configured in an unusual way, and PHP considers it an unlikely risk.

The project is not issuing an emergency fix for it. Instead, it recommends turning off a feature called session upload progress until a fix is available in the next routine release.

The warning came in a short informational advisory published on October 23. It follows the October 21 emergency release that fixed two critical PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which let an attacker without an account run code on a server. Those were patched in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The new issue is separate and is not fixed by those releases.

Only a narrow setup is at risk. PHP says the problem can occur when a web application does all of the following: sets the session.serialize_handler option to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration, then changes that option to php while running by calling ini_set(), and makes that change before it calls session_start().

Session upload progress must also still be turned on. An application that never changes the serialize handler while running can leave the feature on and is not exposed through this path. PHP says this setup is unlikely in practice.

The action is one line. PHP recommends setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next routine bugfix release. This is the same setting it already listed as a mitigation in the October 21 advisory for CVE-2026-109619.

Anyone who applied it then and left it in place needs to do nothing more for the new issue. Session upload progress is turned on by default and lets an application track the progress of a file upload.

Because the setup is uncommon, PHP is handling the fix as part of its regular release cycle rather than as an emergency, and it will publish a full advisory for CVE-2026-115560 with the next release.

PHP has not stated which versions are affected, which releases will contain the fix, or a severity score. It also has not said whether the new issue shares a root cause with CVE-2026-109619.

No exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 has been reported; the attacks reported since October 21 target the two earlier PHP2Shell flaws.

Separately, attempts to exploit the two earlier PHP2Shell flaws have surged. Amazon said its honeypots logged an exploit attempt against CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 on October 17, four days before the flaws were disclosed, and Cloudflare said attempts rose from tens of thousands within 45 minutes of the October 21 disclosure to millions by early October 22.

Attackers have tried to use the flaws to install a Mirai botnet variant, according to Sophos and Arctic Wolf. Those attempts have so far failed: Previdian, Wordfence and others report scanning and probing but no confirmed code execution, and researchers say a reliable exploit is proving harder to build than expected. That activity targets the two flaws patched on October 21, not CVE-2026-115560, which has not been reported under attack.

item.title: Hackers Breach Enterprise Firewalls and VPNs, Exposing Over 70,000 Credentials (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a large-scale campaign that has targeted exposed network edge devices such as Fortinet FortiGate and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect firewalls.

"Artifacts from this investigation also indicate that operators in this campaign have obtained access to numerous organizations worldwide, and have attempted to further compromise some victims, resulting in persistent remote access and data exfiltration," according to a joint investigation published by Group-IB and NyxLab.

The widespread exploitation activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as k0t, who also goes by the aliases CryptoFeel, Member19, and QazWsxShop. The cybercriminal actor was first seen in the wild on October 22, 2025.

The threat actor is assessed to share connections with ransomware groups such as Qilin and The Gentlemen, likely operating as an initial access broker or an affiliate. Analysis of the threat actor's dark web activity reveals a keen interest in purchasing vulnerability exploit code and tools or premium accounts for metadata search engines like FOFA and ZoomEye.

The campaign's victims are global and belong to a broad range of sectors, given the indiscriminate targeting of exposed network devices. A significant chunk of compromises are said to have taken place between February and June 2026, which also overlaps with another credential harvesting campaign codenamed FortiBleed.

Nearly 38% of victims are concentrated in the Asia Pacific region, followed by 31.9% in Latin America, 15.8% in Europe, and 12.7% in the Middle East and North Africa.

The attack chain plays out as follows -

  • Conduct reconnaissance through public scanning tools like FOFA and ZoomEye to enumerate internet-facing VPN and firewall appliances, filter candidates by product, and put together target lists of potentially vulnerable edge devices.
  • Attempt to exploit these devices via known vulnerabilities like CVE-2025-64446 (a path traversal flaw in FortiWeb) and CVE-2026-0257 (an authentication bypass flaw in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Prisma Access) through bespoke Python scripts named "fortnew.py" and "exploit_2026_0257.py," or perform brute-force attacks using common username and password combinations, to obtain initial access.
  • Establish a foothold on the targets via an OpenConnect VPN connection.
  • Conduct post-exploitation actions and additional credential theft like enumeration of Active Directory, SMB, and installed antivirus solution.
  • Establish persistence on the host via legitimate remote access tools like MeshCentral Agent, Atera, Teramind, and AnyDes, as well as an open-source, adversary-emulation framework known as AdaptixC2.
  • Exfiltrate harvested data using Rclone into Wasabi S3 buckets and MEGA cloud drives.

The attacks are also characterized by the use of legitimate administrator and pentesting utilities like NetExec, SoftPerfect, Impacket, noPac, Kerbrute, PetitPotam, and Mimikatz to burrow deeper into victims' corporate environments.

"k0t appears to select potential targets by enumerating exposed network appliances at scale rather than researching individual organizations," Group-IB and NyxLab researchers said. "His stated geographic priorities begin with the United States and Canada, followed by European countries and selected APAC markets."

"The product and location of an exposed device therefore appear to matter more than the industry of the organization operating it, consistent with the broad range of victims observed in this campaign."

k0t's links to Qilin and The Gentlemen stem from the fact that many victims of the campaign were also later listed by the ransomware groups on their data leak sites. However, the exact nature of the connection between the threat and these gangs is unclear.

What's more, Group-IB and NyxLab said they found a "negligible overlap" in compromised data between this activity and FortBleed. More than 70,000 exposed credentials associated with network devices and LDAP dumps have been identified in connection with the campaign.

"This aligns with reports that many operators are likely to be involved in the FortiBleed activity cluster, suggesting that this may be a separate dataset, operator subset, or related access operation within the broader FortiBleed-related activity," the researchers said. "Organizations are advised to act on ensuring that any vulnerabilities mentioned in this report are appropriately remedied."

item.title: Exposed Infrastructure Reveals How Ransomware Affiliates Used AI Agents to Execute Intrusions (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have discovered an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven intrusion ecosystem run by affiliates of the INC and The Gentlemen ransomware groups.

Central to the operation is an "Autonomous Red Team Kill Chain Framework" referred to as Phantom. The threat actor is assessed to be Russian-speaking and functions both as an intrusion and data-extortion operator, as well as an infrastructure provider supporting different partners across the ransomware ecosystem.

"The operators exploited edge and remote-access systems at scale, including FortiClient EMS, SimpleHelp, cPanel, and VPN gateways," SOCRadar said. "They used AI-managed knowledge bases to track victims, stolen credentials, and campaign progress."

A notable aspect that defines the campaign is its "AI-executed, human-approved operating structure" in which a human operator provides a victim-specific prompt and reviews every step, while the intrusions themselves are executed through OpenCode with OpenRouter-hosted commercial models.

An examination of the exposed directory at 45.227.254[.]43 has revealed the activity logged 8,257 messages across 133 sessions. Should the models refuse to act on the prompts, the operator has been found to rewrite requests as an authorized red team assessment instead of simply switching models.

Initial access is achieved by exploiting public-facing edge devices at scale, following which the attackers move laterally, establish persistence, exfiltrate data, and escalate toward ransomware deployment. Operator records indicate that the attacks involve the exploitation of the following flaws -

  • CVE-2024-57727 (SimpleHelp path traversal) (Actively exploited)
  • CVE-2026-35616 (Fortinet FortiClient authentication bypass) (Actively exploited)
  • CVE-2026-41940 (cPanel/WHM authentication bypass) (Actively exploited)
  • CVE-2026-15409 (SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF) (Staged for targeting, no confirmed compromise)
  • CVE-2026-63030 (WordPress wp2shell) (Developed)
  • CVE-2026-42208 (LiteLLM SQL injection) (Developed or referenced)
  • CVE-2026-9082 (Drupal SQL injection) (Developed or referenced)

"Once inside, the operators followed a recurring lifecycle: enumerate the domain, escalate to domain admin where possible, harvest credentials with stealer tooling, prioritize finance, HR, legal and executive files, and collect them over reverse-SOCKS tunnels," SOCRadar said.

"Credential reuse was the main force multiplier; in one case, a single reused password unlocked the VPN, servers, RMM, backup and security management platforms at once. Security products were impaired with a BYOVD killer and loader-level evasion, although the operators' own logs record mixed results against enterprise EDRs."

Supporting the threat actor in their goals is a diverse toolkit comprising bespoke frameworks, modified open-source tools, and compiled binaries -

  • Phantom, an AI-powered offensive security and penetration testing framework that's deployed in live operations via OpenCode and employs an agent that communicates with an external server to retrieve tasks, execute commands, and return outputs. It supports 18 skill modules to facilitate reconnaissance, binary reverse engineering, exploit research, steganography, telemetry assessment, and EDR fingerprinting, among others.
  • WormGPT-MCP, a set of 32 Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers connecting the AI system to 32 different modules that span functions ranging from reconnaissance to extortion.
  • Ghost C2, a collection of three generations of polymorphic implants that communicate with a remote server over Cloudflare, Telegram, or DNS, and execute tasking and maintain persistent beacons on compromised endpoints.
  • RevSocks, a reverse SOCKS5 framework used to pivot inside victim networks and stage data for exfiltration.

Other tools include a Cloudflare-fronted Mythic agent dubbed QuickLine, a Quick Heal/Seqrite EDR killer that abuses the Zemana driver ("zam64.sys") as part of a BYOVD attack, and exfiltration programs such as rks3 and BackupAgent.

Analysis of dozens of AI-authored extortion records shows that the threat actors adopt a data-centric approach. It involves examining the stolen financials to determine the amount a victim can pay without having to involve a bank or an insurer, and then sending masked proof samples and ramping up pressure through scripted vishing calls and threatening to notify customers, partners, and regulators.

The stolen data is eventually published on the data leak site if the victim fails to pay within a 24-72 hour deadline. That said, the final outcomes of these ransom demands are unknown as no cryptocurrency wallet or payment record has been recovered.

A total of 62 organizations are estimated to have been targeted by the operation, out of which four of them ended up being listed on the data leak sites for INC and The Gentlemen ransomware. The U.S. accounts for more than 50% of the targets. The attacks also primarily targeted industrial, manufacturing, and energy sectors, followed by healthcare and pharmaceutical organizations.

"Across this exposed infrastructure, the actors engaged in widespread exploitation of exposed internet services, specifically targeting FortiClient EMS gateways, Ivanti/Citrix/SonicWall/OpenVPN gateways, SimpleHelp remote management servers, and cPanel hosting controls," SOCRadar said.

"Concurrently, they orchestrated operations via the Phantom framework, established RevSocks reverse-SOCKS proxies for network pivoting, deployed Ghost C2 variants, and utilized AI-managed knowledge bases to meticulously log victim telemetry, compromised credentials, and active campaign statuses."

item.title: Ruby Fixes Three Regex Engine Bugs Responsible for Four Critical GitLab RCE Flaws (2026)
item.description:
Ruby has released versions 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13 to fix three bugs in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into the language. The bugs lie behind four critical security flaws that GitLab patched over the past month.

GitLab found that a specially crafted pattern could corrupt memory while Ruby compiles it, potentially leading to code execution on its own servers.

Ruby says any application that builds a regular expression from text an attacker controls is affected, not just GitLab.

Which Applications Are Affected

In its advisory, Ruby said an application is affected only if it compiles a regular expression from a string an attacker controls. That happens when a program passes such a string to Regexp.new, Regexp.union or Regexp.compile, or places it inside a pattern through interpolation, as in /#{input}/.

Applications that only use regular expressions written by their own developers are not affected.

Ruby fixed the bugs in 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13. The 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 releases are the first in their series to carry any of the three fixes.

  • Ruby 4.0: upgrade to 4.0.9
  • Ruby 3.4: upgrade to 3.4.12
  • Ruby 3.3: upgrade to 3.3.13

An earlier release from the same week, 4.0.8, does not include the fix for one of the flaws, CVE-2026-110264, so 4.0 users should install 4.0.9.

Ruby 3.2 and earlier will not get a fix. Ruby 3.2 reached end of life on April 1, 2026, and 3.2.11 was its final release. Ruby recommends moving to 3.4 or 4.0.

If you cannot upgrade yet, the advisory says to stop compiling regular expressions from untrusted input.

Two defenses that look like they would help do not. Setting Regexp.timeout does not stop these bugs. Capping the length of a pattern is also unreliable because short patterns can trigger bugs.

How the Bugs Reached GitLab

GitLab compiles regular expressions supplied by its users, such as the patterns in a CI/CD configuration. It found that crafted patterns could corrupt memory as Ruby compiled them, and it issued four CVEs between September 23 and October 21, fixing each by shipping a patched Ruby.

The first two, disclosed on September 23, each need a logged-in account and were rated 9.9 out of 10. The two from October, CVE-2026-97229 on the 12th and CVE-2026-110264 on the 21st, need no account and were rated 10.0, the maximum. CVE-2026-110264 reaches every GitLab version from 7.0 onward.

A researcher using the handle joaxcar reported all four through GitLab's bug bounty program. As of October 23, none of the four was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

No Ruby CVE, for Now

Ruby has not requested CVE identifiers of its own for these fixes, "at least for now," it said, and told users to track the issues by GitLab's four CVE numbers instead.

That leaves a gap for anyone who scans by CVE. GitLab's CVE records name only GitLab as the affected product, so a scanner that checks those records against installed Ruby versions has nothing to match.

Ruby has treated this kind of bug as a vulnerability before, assigning CVE numbers to fixes in 2022 and 2024, even though it has long been unsafe to build a regular expression from untrusted input.

Its documentation still describes untrusted patterns only as a denial-of-service risk. Ruby said it will update its advisory if it requests any CVE identifiers.

For GitLab Administrators

Self-managed GitLab instances need the release that fixes CVE-2026-110264. GitLab shipped it on October 21 and backported it as far as version 18.11.13.

  • 19.5.1
  • 19.4.3
  • 19.3.6
  • 19.2.9
  • 19.1.9
  • 19.0.10
  • 18.11.13

GitLab.com already runs the patched version, and GitLab Dedicated tenants on recent internal releases need no action, GitLab said. Because GitLab bundles its own copy of Ruby and patched it there, installing one of these fixed versions applies the fix.

GitLab also published detection rules that self-managed administrators can use to look for signs of exploitation attempts.

item.title: BlackX UEFI Bootkit Bypasses Secure Boot on Patched Windows Systems Missing Revocations (2026)
item.description:
Diplomatic organizations in Central Asia have been targeted by a sophisticated new Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) bootkit called BlackX.

The activity, which singled out diplomatic entities in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan in early 2026, is suspected to be orchestrated by a China-linked state-sponsored hacking group known as APT41, Kaspersky said in a technical report published this week.

The primary objective behind deploying the malware is to undermine Microsoft Windows startup defenses, along with third-party security solutions, while maintaining long-term, covert access to compromised devices.

Notably, BlackX is assessed to be an updated version of BlackLotus, a notorious bootkit that was first observed being advertised on cybercrime forums in late 2022, before its existence was officially confirmed by ESET in March 2023.

BlackLotus is designed to exploit a now-patched Secure Boot bypass vulnerability tracked as CVE-2022-21894 (CVSS score: 4.4), also known as Baton Drop, to load malicious code before the operating system starts. However, successful exploitation hinges on an attacker having administrator privileges or physical access to a target host.

"It is critical to note that a threat actor's use of this bootkit is primarily a persistence and defense evasion mechanism," Microsoft noted at the time. "It is not a first-stage payload or an initial access vector and can only be deployed to a device to which a threat actor has already gained either privileged access or physical access."

That said, completely addressing the threat requires additional actions beyond installing the latest update, including running manual steps to apply Microsoft's Secure Boot revocation mitigations, such as adding the "Windows Production PCA 2011" certificate to the Secure Boot UEFI Forbidden List (DBX).

The Russian cybersecurity company has found that attackers are capitalizing on the fact that organizations have not carried out these manual steps, allowing them to continue using the Baton Drop vulnerability even on systems where the "patch" has been applied.

"On October 19, 2026, this certificate expired, but this does not prevent the vulnerable binaries from loading unless the certificate is blocklisted," researchers Georgy Kucherin, Vladimir Nestor, and Vasily Berdnikov said.

"It is likely that the threat actor behind this campaign took into account that few organizations realized the importance of manually activating the Baton Drop patch. As such, we believe they decided to invest time in understanding how BlackLotus works and creating a copycat of this bootkit."

Attackers have been observed deploying BlackX after breaching victim networks through an unspecified method and gaining administrator privileges. To install the bootkit, the threat actor drops the following files -

  • inst.exe, an installer executable
  • PVMDIJGKAX2, an encrypted extensionless file containing files and strings required for the installation

The installer is then launched via the command line as "C:\ProgramData\Intel\inst.exe PVMDIJGKAX2 Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1," where "Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1" is the RC4 key used for decryption.

The binary then drops additional files to both system and UEFI partitions to exploit CVE-2022-21894 in a manner that's "remarkably similar" to the one used in BlackLotus. The end goal remains the same: install Machine Owner Keys (MOK) to load arbitrary EFI files on the infected hosts and interfere with Secure Boot.

What's noteworthy here is that the complete source code of BlackLotus has never been made publicly available, indicating that the threat actors behind BlackX either reverse-engineered the original bootkit or purchased its source code from another party.

"Either way, this is an interesting observation, as we rarely see APT actors borrow ideas or code from cybercrime actors," Kaspersky said.

The UEFI payload delivered following the exploitation of the vulnerability is engineered to inject a malicious driver into the Windows kernel. The driver has been signed with a certificate belonging to a company named Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio. The certificate has since been revoked by the issuer.

Like in the case of the bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) attack, the driver attempts to tamper with the functioning of endpoint security software installed on the machine. In an interesting twist, some of the unauthorized modifications are allowed to run only if security programs associated with Kaspersky or Avast are present. However, Kaspersky's analysis has found these routines to be ineffective.

Not just content with trying to render security solutions ineffective, the driver also drops a user-mode payload for cyber espionage. Two such payloads have been observed -

  • A remote access trojan that can deliver additional .NET payloads, while using Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk for command-and-control (C2) to blend in with regular enterprise workflows. It's also equipped to harvest system information and upload files of interest.
  • A malicious DLL dubbed OxiDLLRunner that's sideloaded by the legitimate "googleupdate.exe" binary, which is also delivered by the bootkit. The DLL decrypts and launches a Rust payload that communicates with "archivetj[.]com" to receive and execute more DLL plugins.

BlackX's connections to APT41 stem from an ESET report in June 2026, which documented FishMonger's use of a Windows backdoor called SprySOCKS in attacks targeting government entities in Honduras, Taiwan, Thailand, and Pakistan between 2023 and 2024. FishMonger, also tracked as Aquatic Panda and Earth Lusca, is assessed to be operating under the APT41 umbrella.

The Slovakian cybersecurity company said it had found "limited indications" that some versions of the backdoor may feature a UEFI bootkit component likely exploiting CVE‑2023‑24932, a bypass for the mitigations introduced by Microsoft to fix CVE-2022-21894. It represents a downgrade attack in which a privileged attacker can force the operating system to boot using an older, legitimately Microsoft-signed version of the Windows Boot Manager to reintroduce CVE-2022-21894.

An interesting overlap is the presence of the "xdd" string in BlackX and the kernel implant used by FishMonger, raising the possibility that the UEFI bootkit used in those attacks is none other than BlackX. The second clue that points to China-aligned hackers is the use of DLL sideloading to deploy the payloads – a pattern that's extremely common among threat actors of Chinese origin.

"By adapting a commercial crimeware tool, the group could bypass procedures intended to protect the Windows boot processes," Kucherin said. "This hybrid approach proves that sophisticated adversaries do not need to reinvent the wheel to establish persistent, invisible control over high-value networks."

item.title: CISA Flags Two Actively Exploited Critical Flaws in Collabora Online and Arista VeloCloud (2026)
item.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added two vulnerabilities impacting Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server and Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing reports of active exploitation in the wild.

The critical-severity vulnerabilities are listed below -

  • CVE-2026-110447 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Collabora Online – Built-in CODE Server (aka richdocumentscode) when used within the NextCloud platform that could allow remote code execution via "proxy.php" when the CODE local document server isn't running. (Fixed in September 2026 in version 26.4.303)
  • CVE-2026-114625 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An SQL injection vulnerability in on-premise versions of Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator that could allow a remote attacker to access privileged internal functionality. (Fixed in October 2026  in versions 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10, and 6.4.2.12)

As reported by The Hacker News, threat actors have been observed exploiting CVE-2026-110447 to backdoor Nextcloud servers with a web shell so as to conduct reconnaissance and search for credential stores, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets.

As for CVE-2026-114625, successful exploitation requires an attacker to have network access to the VCO web interface and a valid authenticated session on the VCO portal. The minimum user role required is Enterprise Read Only.

Although Arista has acknowledged that the vulnerability is "known to be actively exploited," it has not attributed the activity to a particular threat actor or provided technical details on how the vulnerability is being exploited and what actions the attackers took after privilege escalation. The company also has not disclosed the number of affected organizations.

However, it has shared two IP addresses geolocated to Japan as responsible for driving the activity -

  • 74.82.197[.]86
  • 38.54.50[.]151

CVE-2026-114625 is the third vulnerability in the same product to have been weaponized in the wild since July 2026, following CVE-2026-16812 (CVSS score: 10.0) and CVE-2026-93952 (CVSS score: 10.0).

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by October 26, 2026, to secure their networks.

item.title: Researchers Push Over 2 Million Updates to Remotely Disable Popcorn Time Updater That Could Fuel a Botnet (2026)
item.description:
Between November 2025 and March 2026, the Dutch security firm Eye Security pushed more than 2 million updates to computers it did not own to switch off a background updater that it said could have allowed an outsider to take over the machine.

The updater belongs to Time4Popcorn, an abandoned copy of Popcorn Time, a free app that streamed pirated films and TV over BitTorrent.

Popcorn Time was popular about a decade ago, and the original shut down in 2014, but several copies kept running under the same name. A separate, legal project that took the Popcorn Time name in early 2025 is unrelated to it.

Eye Security, which monitors client networks for threats, found the updater during a routine threat hunt: a program called Updater.exe on one client's laptop kept trying to reach a web address that was no longer registered.

The firm registered the address itself to see what would connect, and about 50 requests a second poured in. It later laid out the operation, which it named Operation IXIM, in a write-up and a talk at Hack.lu on October 22.

Over six months, those requests carried more than 3.8 million different hardware IDs. The IDs proved an unreliable way to count machines, because some Windows PCs shared one and some Macs changed theirs, so Eye revised its estimate to 2.5 to 3 million Windows computers and 250,000 to 350,000 Macs.

The updater ran in the background on Windows and Mac from the moment the computer started. It checked for new versions over an unencrypted connection and installed whatever it was sent, at the highest privilege level, called SYSTEM on Windows and root on Mac, without checking who sent it.

Because the web addresses it called had been abandoned, Eye said, anyone who registered the right one could have served their own program to every machine still calling it.

On a machine with that access, an attacker could install ransomware, steal saved passwords, or pull the computer into a botnet, Eye said. Mapping a sample of the connecting addresses, the firm said it saw home users around the world, as well as machines on government, military, and corporate networks, though it added that it is "hard to draw conclusions" from that.

Eye had disclosed the flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-30612, in June. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency rates it 9.8 out of 10. It affects three versions of the Time4Popcorn software:

  • Windows, up to and including 6.2.1.18
  • Mac, up to and including 6.2.1.17
  • Android, up to and including 3.5.0.173

Turning the Updater Against Itself

With no company left to fix the software and no patch coming, Eye decided to use the updater against itself. After taking legal advice, it served the machines an update that does one thing: it stops and disables the updater, deleting no files and collecting nothing.

Eye compared the step to Operation Ladybird in 2021, when Dutch police pushed an update to computers infected with the Emotet botnet to disable the malware on them.

The difference, Eye said, is that Emotet's victims never chose to be infected, while Popcorn Time's users installed the app themselves. Still, the firm said, "none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years."

Soon after the updates began, someone uploaded Eye's update to VirusTotal, and antivirus engines started flagging it as malware, a fair description of a program that disables a Windows service. Because every product that blocked it left the vulnerable updater running, Eye reworked the update until only one scanner continued to flag it.

By December 2025, Eye had updated more than 1 million systems and cut the traffic to its web addresses by about 90 percent. By March 1, it was sending about 5,000 updates a day, a 98 percent reduction. Judging the remaining numbers too small to interest a botnet operator, Eye stopped, having sent more than 2 million update downloads in all.

In late March, Eye handed the 15 web addresses it controlled to the Shadowserver Foundation, a non-profit that takes abandoned and malicious domains out of circulation, so a trusted party would hold them rather than Eye.

Public registration records for one of them, popcorntimeupd[.]xyz, now point to Shadowserver's sinkhole servers, with a transfer dated March 20, 2026. Other addresses the updater calls were never Eye's to take and remain with outside owners, the firm said, so machines that reach those are still exposed.

Eye found no sign that anyone else was serving code through the addresses: the ones already registered by other people were parked or up for sale, not pushing updates to the machines calling them. The flaw is not listed in CISA's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities as of October 23, 2026.

What Popcorn Time Users Should Do

Switching off the updater does not make the app safe. Eye said Popcorn Time runs on a 2014 browser engine with its security sandbox turned off, loads content over unencrypted connections, and pulls in code from other abandoned web addresses.

Eye registered those abandoned addresses too, which it said would have let it run its own code on every machine that opened the app. It did not, but it built a working proof of concept, so the risk is real. item.title: Google Says Gmail and Photos Data Shared With AI Search Could Be Used for Targeted Ads (2026)
item.description:
Google has updated its privacy policy to spell out that using personalized artificial intelligence (AI) features in Search or Gemini could allow the company to serve targeted ads to users based on their activity on other connected Google services.

"You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service," reads a policy update effective October 16, 2026.

"For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads."

Google also notes in its revised policy that "We don't show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos, unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads."

News of the policy update was first reported by Android Authority.

Personal Intelligence, unveiled by Google in Gemini in January 2026, allows users to connect other services like Gmail, Google Photos, and YouTube as a way to provide tailored answers in combination with their chat history preferences.

The feature is currently rolling out as a beta to eligible users over the age of 18 globally, except in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, the U.K., and Nigeria.

It's worth noting that the policy states it doesn't use content from Gmail, Drive, or Photos to personalize ads by default. However, that changes should users opt to share photos or emails with AI Mode and other Search tools via the Personal Intelligence feature.

In other words, if users interact with AI Mode or Gemini while Personal Intelligence is enabled, the data that informs those answers (i.e., content from Gmail or Photos) could be used as a signal to serve targeted ads. The privacy policy aims to make it clear that feeding personal data into its AI tools could contribute to ad personalization.

Users should be mindful of the privacy trade-off when connecting their apps to enable AI features. Those who prefer to opt out can do so by selecting the apps they want to disconnect from Personal Intelligence or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings ("www.google[.]com/search-personalization").

In January 2026, OpenAI began showing ads to logged-in adult U.S. users in both the free and ChatGPT Go tiers, while emphasizing that users' data and conversations are protected and never sold to advertisers. It has also said the ads do not influence responses from the chatbot, and that users are in control of the experience.

Earlier this week, the AI company said it's expanded advertising on ChatGPT to 26 more countries, ​bringing the total to 89. This includes 14 more ​Latin American countries and several markets across Europe, Africa, and Asia.

"We keep conversations private from advertisers and do not sell customer data," OpenAI stressed. "Ads in ChatGPT are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT's answers, and advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides."
